item.title: NFL news, live updates: Browns QB Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol; Tyler Huntley to miss remainder of season, Joe Fagnano to start Week 9
item.description: Follow along with the latest NFL news coming out of Week 8.
item.content:encoded:
We’re gearing up for Week 9 of the NFL season (and the looming NFL trade deadline), where teams will have to make a decision on the intended course of the remainder of their season — are they going all in? Or is it time to tear it all down and look toward the future?

One of those teams will be the Baltimore Ravens (4-4), whose quarterback, Lamar Jackson, suffered a thumb injury that will require surgery and has landed him on injured reserve. Backup Tyler Huntley then suffered what is reportedly a season-ending turf toe injury in relief of Jackson, putting undrafted free agent Joe Fagnano into action as the emergency third quarterback.

Now, Fagnano will get the start as the Jacksonville Jaguars travel to face the Ravens on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 9. The 25-year-old, who played his college ball at Maine and then UConn, will be the second undrafted rookie to start under center for Baltimore in the Ravens' 32-year history, per ESPN's Jamison Hensley.

NFL fans also await news on the fate of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who has been touted as a potential trade-deadline mover as the Indianapolis Colts kicked off their franchise reset with a fire sale. They’ve already traded away two foundational players, Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner, for several draft picks as they look to the future, leaving us to wonder whether their star running back could be next.

Follow along with Yahoo Sports for the latest NFL news, injury updates and more ahead of Week 9.

item.title: Former Seahawks draft pick has become one of the NFL’s unlikely sack leaders
item.description: There are only eight players with at least six sacks entering Week 9 of the NFL season, and one of those players is a former Seahawk.
item.content:encoded:
One of the few bright spots on yet another very bad Tennessee Titans team is a former Seattle Seahawks pass rusher.

Jacob Martin, a 2018 sixth-round pick who was famously part of the Jadeveon Clowney trade just prior to the 2019 regular season, has hung around in the NFL for nearly a decade. He’s been a rotational pass rusher with the Seahawks, Houston Texans, New York Jets, Denver Broncos, Indianapolis Colts, Washington Commanders, and now he finds himself in Nashville for his ninth season.

It’s also his best season to date; one that has him as one of the NFL’s best at sacking the quarterback.

After taking Joe Burrow down not once, not twice, but three times in Tennessee’s wild 43-36 overtime loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, Martin has already reached a career-high 6.5 sacks through eight games. Only T.J. Watt, Will Anderson, Chase Young, and Greg Rousseau have more sacks than Martin.

At 30 years old, Martin appears to be the definition of a late bloomer. He had 5.5 sacks last season with the Commanders, and as a starter on the Titans he’s putting up very impressive numbers under Robert Saleh. Martin leads the Titans with 21 pressures, his 7 quick pressures (which is a pressure within 2.5 seconds) puts him on pace to match if not surpass his previous career high of 16. He already has 14 QB hits, which is only four fewer than all of last season, and his tackles for loss is already at a career high. The only thing to note is his pressure rate of 11.4% is modest, but he’s turning his pressures into sacks, and his one-year, $9 million contract looks like it’ll parlay into a bigger deal next offseason… an offseason in which Seattle will likely be overhauling its edge rush unit.

Meanwhile, fellow former Seahawk Boye Mafe recorded a strip-sack of Cam Ward in the same game, bringing his total to 5.5 on the season for the Bengals. His first season in Cincinnati is looking like one of the best of his career, and the Bengals should be in good shape to return to the playoffs given their remaining schedule.

Good for both of them!

item.title: Bills vs Ravens game balls: Far from perfect but several players stepped up for Buffalo
item.description: Handing out game balls for Buffalo’s win over the Baltimore
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills came out of their bye with plenty to celebrate. A rookie cornerback collected his first career interception. Josh Allen passed a franchise legend. And a defense that had spent too many afternoons trying to hang on finally gave its head coach a reason to celebrate the finish.

Buffalo’s 36–10 win over the Baltimore Ravens moved the Bills to 6–1, with Joe Brady’s postgame game balls recognizing individual milestones and a collective response.

Baltimore’s quarterback injuries are part of the story. Lamar Jackson left after the Ravens’ first offensive play, and Tyler Huntley later exited as well. But Buffalo still had to capitalize, and this time the defense did more than make an occasional play.

Official game-ball recipients

Davison Igbinosun

Igbinosun’s first career interception came with a little help and plenty of awareness. Late in the second quarter, a pass bounced off Geno Stone’s hands and helmet, leaving the football hanging in the air. Igbinosun tracked it, secured the interception and returned it 17 yards, giving Buffalo another scoring opportunity before halftime.

The rookie played 41 defensive snaps and made his opportunity count. In the locker room, Igbinosun thanked God and his teammates for pushing him to become “the best version of myself,” closing with a simple, “Go Bills.”

A first interception is a milestone on its own. Bass turning it into 3 points before halftime made it even better.

Josh Allen

Allen’s game ball recognized a milestone that deserves a moment of its own.

His 11-yard touchdown pass to DJ Moore in the fourth quarter was the 259th of his Bills career, including postseason games, moving him past Jim Kelly’s 258 for the franchise record. Allen added another touchdown pass to Dalton Kincaid later in the quarter.

Allen finished 21-of-34 passing for 289 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. He also rushed for 30 yards and the game’s opening touchdown.

Kelly has been the standard against which generations of Buffalo quarterbacks have been measured. But Allen continues to rewrite the record book and has become the new standard.

It wasn’t a flawless afternoon, but it was another reminder of the legacy Allen has built and continues building in Buffalo.

The Defense

Brady’s third game ball went to the defense, with Bradley Chubb called forward to accept it on behalf of the group.

“145 total yards, 3 takeaways, 4 sacks…and we finished,” Brady said. “Defense the way you respond. How we practiced. You earned it. Bradley Chubb. Here we go baby.”

Cole Bishop’s strip-sack led to a fumble recovery by Kaleb Elarms-Orr. Igbinosun added the interception, and Dorian Williams recovered Baltimore’s other lost fumble. Buffalo finished with four sacks, 12 quarterback hits and three takeaways, holding the Ravens to 3-of-13 on third down.

The Bills also limited Derrick Henry to 53 rushing yards and held Zay Flowers without a reception on five targets.

Yes, Baltimore’s injuries changed the matchup. But Buffalo took advantage instead of allowing an undermanned opponent to hang around.

After several games where the defense struggled to close the door, the finish was worth recognizing.

Honorable mentions

Tyler Bass

Bass made all three field goals, connecting from 56, 22 and 51 yards, and converted all three extra-point attempts.

Dalton Kincaid

Kincaid led Buffalo with 86 receiving yards on four catches, averaging 21.5 yards per reception. 

His afternoon included a 40-yard gain and the 23-yard fourth-quarter touchdown that pushed Buffalo’s lead to 36–10.

Damar Hamlin

With C.J. Gardner-Johnson suspended, Hamlin played all 51 defensive snaps, finishing with five combined tackles and a pass defensed. He was the only Bills defender who never came off the field.

A full workload alone doesn’t earn an honorable mention. But handling that responsibility in a secondary that held Baltimore to 91 gross passing yards deserves recognition.

DJ Moore

In his return to the lineup, Moore caught four passes for 82 yards and a touchdown, including a 49-yard reception that helped spark Buffalo’s second-half offense.

Khalil Shakir

Shakir hauled in five receptions for 64 yards, providing a reliable target for Josh Allen and helping move the chains.

Te’Cory Couch

With Buffalo’s secondary shorthanded, Couch stepped up for 36 defensive snaps (71%), recording four combined tackles and helping the Bills limit Baltimore’s passing attack.

The game balls celebrated a first, a franchise record and a collective response. Next comes Minnesota, where Buffalo will need to prove that finishing was more than a one-week improvement.

item.title: AP Chiefs Mailbag: What to think of the Kingsley Suamataia mess?
item.description: Arrowhead Pride staff writer Jared Sapp answers your questions about Kansas City after a disheartening loss.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag!Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs!

A frustrating loss to the Denver Broncos dropped the Chiefs to 5-2 and left fans wondering how seriously to panic. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds ahead of hopefully a get-right opportunity against the New York Jets.

Tomahawk0611 asks:


Why didn’t left guard Kingsley Suamataia play yesterday? Has he been permanently benched?

We saw Suamataia benched in Week 4 only to return to the starting lineup after the bye. I suspect that we will see him again in Week 9 against the Jets, but this has been a weird situation.

I think it is fair to be frustrated with Reid’s cryptic responses, but what should be obvious is that the staff has made it clear to the player they are not happy about something. It is unclear whether that is tied to performance or practice habits.

Whatever the problem, however, I don’t think fans are putting enough blame on Suamataia for how he is falling short of expectations. This is especially true considering one of the biggest fan criticisms from the past few seasons has been a perceived lack of accountability.

The frustration with the staff and front office should be that they did not have a better backup plan than Mike Caliendo before deciding to hold the line on Suamataia.

GoldenDomer asks:


Is the QB sneak refusal an Andy Reid thing or Patrick Mahomes thing? It’s equally disappointing that Mahomes hasn’t just done it on his own at this point.

Since the night in Denver that the world saw Mahomes’ kneecap put back into place on the field, the quarterback sneak has clearly not been an option for the Chiefs. We saw the team briefly use tight end Noah Gray — and Blake Bell before him — on the play. Unfortunately, teams quickly caught on.

For fans, the obvious answer to short-yardage woes has been to re-sign running back Kareem Hunt. My solution would be to put backup quarterback Justin Fields into some third-and-1 and fourth-and-1 plays. Perhaps that means taking Mahomes off the field for a snap. Perhaps that has both quarterbacks on the field at the same time. Defenses accounting for Fields would likely pay bigger dividends for running backs Kenneth Walker and Emmett Johnson in the crucial situations.

Glorified KC asks:


Why did the defense struggle so much in the fourth quarter? Did Sean Payton figure out a weakness to exploit? They went from allowing 0 first downs in the third quarter to allowing 15 points in the fourth.

To be fair, the Chiefs are not the only team to have trouble putting the Broncos away late. Of Denver’s now six wins, they were trailing or tied entering the fourth quarter four times (with one of their other wins coming in overtime). I assumed that the Jacksonville Jaguars and Los Angeles Rams would put the Broncos away, only to see a similar story unfold that we saw Sunday.

Reid put the defense in bad positions twice by punting on fourth-and-1, leading to a touchback, before having Harrison Butker miss a 54-yard field goal to start Denver’s final position at their own 44-yard line. I actually think Reid chose the wrong time to punt in either situation.

On both of Denver’s touchdown drives, the Chiefs’ defense surrendered a massive play. One saw a 15-yard penalty added on, and the final drive saw a 50-yard play go to the five-yard line.

The defense let Kansas City down. However, I would also put heavy blame on conservative offensive playcalling that yielded zero points in the final frame.

Atypical Vagabond asks:


Can the Chiefs stop beating themselves? There is no reason not to win with a 15 point lead… yet we certainly found a way to lose.

There are two seasons that are coming to mind when I see how the last two weeks have gone.

The first season I covered the Chiefs for Arrowhead Pride was 2021. That year, the Chiefs appeared to play undisciplined much of the season and had a predictable offense where almost anyone could tell what play was about to be called based on the formation. That season ended with an inexcusable loss in the AFC Championship game.

The other season I am thinking of came in 2023, when Kansas City took an extended offensive slump almost to the playoffs, including an inept Christmas Day performance against the Raiders. We will remember that year ended with Kansas City’s third Super Bowl title in a five-season span.

The past two games have been frustrating. However, I think we need to wait out the rest of the slate and judge the Chiefs on the whole of the season. That said, we need to see the team really focus on getting right over the next three weeks against a trio of seemingly lesser opponents.

RunningFree asks:

At what point will (local) media turn on Andy’s way of not providing meaningful answers no matter the question?

If someone asked him if it rained during the game at Denver he might say something along the lines of:

“We’ll go back, look at the tape, and see where we’re at. I’m not gonna get into all the details on that. You guys saw what happened out there. So, uh, we’ll just go from there.”

Truthfully, I included this question because it really made me laugh.

I do not know how much longer the 68-year-old Reid plans to continue coaching. But I don’t see him changing his tone with the media.

Fans frequently vent frustration that beat writers are not asking tough enough questions when Reid is available, typically on Wednesdays, Fridays, and after games. I would counter that most of those writers know what topics Reid is likely to be more upfront about. It is hard to create content off of the coach’s nonanswers.

Local media will continue to ask similar questions in press conferences. When we do get unflattering details around the team — such as what we have seen recently with tackle Josh Simmons — expect national media to continue breaking the news.

Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! We will be back after the Chiefs try to get back on track against the Jets. Keep watchingThe Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.

item.title: Texans Sign DT Naquan Jones
item.description: The former Texans DT is returning to Houston after a stint on the 49ers’ practice squad.
item.content:encoded:
The Texans are making more midseason moves at defensive tackle. On Monday morning, the team announced that they are signing former Houston Texan DT Naquan Jones from the San Francisco 49ers’ practice squad:

In a coinciding move, the Texans are also waiving DT Jaden Crumedy. Crumedy, 26, was signed by Texans off of the Green Bay Packers’ practice squad on September 11th, following rookie DT Kayden McDonald’s placement on IR to begin the season. Crumedy would appear in six games for the Texans, tallying six tackles, a QB hit, half a sack, and a 53.8 PFF Grade (51.4 RDEF, 71.4 TACK, 59.4 PRSH) in 87 snaps on defense. As of today, Crumedy has cleared waivers and is being signed to Houston’s practice squad.

Naquan Jones, who is returning to the Texans after failing to make the initial 53-man roster, returns after a brief stint with the San Francisco 49ers, where he appeared in three games and tallied two tackles, one pressure, and a 29.5 PFF Grade (33.0 RDEF, 28.4 TACK, 52.5 PRSH) in 44 snaps on defense. He will replace Crumedy on the DT depth chart. The current lineup consists of:

  • Sheldon Rankins
  • Tommy Togiai
  • Kayden McDonald
  • Logan Hall
  • Naquan Jones
  • Mario Edwards Jr. (Season-Ending IR)

Crumedy may not have been a complete disaster for the Texans, but he does not offer the veteran experience that Jones has, especially considering he played over 100 snaps in Houston’s final month of action in 2025. 

Following Houston’s 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants, it was clear that improvements had to be made in stopping the run before every team starts copying the Giants’ playbook against the Texans. At 6’ 3” and 313 lbs., Jones should plug right into the LDT spot, next to Logan Hall, Sheldon Rankins, Tommy Togiai, or Kayden McDonald depending on the situation. Hopefully, he’ll pick up where he left off in Houston last year as a solid, if unspectacular interior defender that possesses enough strength and speed to be a handful for opposing offensive lineman. His experience in DeMeco Ryans/Matt Burke’s scheme should give him a chance to make an impact right away, which could be great news if he and McDonald are able to complement each other. 

In addition to the Naquan Jones signing, the Texans are also signing UDFA RB Joshua Pitsenberger to the practice squad and releasing RB Deuce Vaughn. They also claimed former Cowboys RB Emari Demercado off waivers last week. Lastly, the Texans also announced today that UDFA WR Daniel Sobkowicz is also joining the practice squad along with Jaden Crumedy, and they are releasing 2025 7th round pick DT Kyonte Hamilton and TE Zaire Mitchell-Paden.

What do you think of these moves? Are the Texans a better team with Naquan Jones on the roster instead of Jaden Crumedy, or was this a mistake? Will Joshua Pitsenberger and/or Emari Demercado contribute on special teams or the offense this coming weekend, or will we all just be anxiously waiting for RB David Montgomery’s return from injury? Let us know your thoughts down in the comments below!

Go Texans!

item.title: Jack Campbell injury update: Latest on Lions LB's condition, status
item.description: Detroit Lions linebacker Jack Campbell suffered a neck injury during a Nov. 1 game. Here's the latest on his condition and recovery.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions are continuing to pray for positive news following Jack Campbell's neck injury.

Updates, especially concrete ones, have been hard to come by in the aftermath of the linebacker's injury, which resulted in him being carted off the field on a backboard during the Lions' Week 8 victory over the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, Nov. 1. Instead, the updates have been more general.

The Lions put out a statement on Nov. 2, saying preliminary results are positive as Campbell continues to rest and recover. Head coach Dan Campbell echoed that statement at his press conference a short time later and explained during a radio interview on Tuesday, Nov. 3 that the linebacker's condition is "improving."

JACK CAMPBELL INJURY UPDATE: Lions share 'positive news' on LB's neck injury

However, the team has yet to mention anything about whether Jack Campbell has movement in his extremities.

Campbell's injury occurred during the fourth quarter on Nov. 1, when making a tackle against Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. He remained motionless on the ground after the hit, where he was attended to by training staff and medical personnel. The linebacker was eventually carted off the field and taken to a local Detroit hospital.

Here's the latest on Campbell's injury and current condition:

Jack Campbell injury update

Dan Campbell provided another small update on Jack Campbell's status during a Tuesday, Nov. 3, radio appearance on 97.1 The Ticket.

"It's not easy because he's always going to be on our minds over here," Dan Campbell said of Jack Campbell, when addressing the Lions' preparation for Week 9. "The good news is he is improving."

The Lions coach made it clear he is providing his players with updates about Jack Campbell's status through the team's captains.

"I think the thought of him – knowing he's doing better, and I've kept the captains up to date, and they've let the other guys know its good news," Dan Campbell said, referencing how players were reacting to the situation. "I think that helps everybody just get a better handle on all this."

Campbell also added that he is trying to keep his players focused on their upcoming game against the Miami Dolphins, expressing concern that "bad things can happen" if players aren't able to be all-in on their gameday responsibilities.

"All we can do at this point is just continue to pray for Jack," Campbell said. "Put our thoughts on him when we have a minute, and on his family. And it's working, like I said. Because he's improving."

When is Dan Campbell's Nov. 4 press conference?

Detroit Lions Dan Campbell will speak to the media at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 4.

It's unclear if he will have any additional updates on Jack Campbell's status when he gets to the podium. You can follow the presser live on the Lions' YouTube page.

What the Lions have said about Jack Campbell's injury

Dan Campbell's update mirrored the Lions' most recent injury update on their All-Pro linebacker, which came via a statement posted to social media on Monday, Nov. 2.

"Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital. Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time," the team said in its statement.

Jack Campbell continues to rest and recover at a local hospital. Preliminary indications are positive and out of respect for Jack and his family we will not share further information at this time.

— Detroit Lions (@Lions) November 2, 2026

The Lions' head coach provided some good news when he took the podium for his press conference later in the day on Nov. 2. While Campbell didn't share any details about his team's linebacker, he told reporters things were generally positive.

"It's positive," Dan Campbell said. "Your prayers are working. Please continue to do that. We'll leave it at that, so continue to pray for him. But it is positive."

Pressed for more information, Campbell said he couldn't share anything else. He added that he briefed the Lions' captains on the linebacker's latest status after the coach visited him in the hospital, and he said the team "knows what's going on."

"I got to go see him last night," Dan Campbell said. "It was good, it was positive. I got to see his parents, talk to his wife. You know, everybody's in good spirits. It's about the recovery. It's a small setback. That's the family. They're very positive, so that's good in that regard."

REGGIE BROWN: Ex-Lions LB reflects on life-altering injury after Jack Campbell hospitalized

What is Jack Campbell's condition?

The Lions have not provided a concrete update on Campbell’s exact condition. The team said the preliminary results are positive, which Dan Campbell echoed at his press conference on Monday, Nov. 2.

However, the exact nature of Campbell’s neck injury and whether he has movement in his extremities has not been shared.

What happened to Jack Campbell?

Campbell went down with a neck injury after tackling Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson in the fourth quarter.

He stayed down as the training staff and medical personnel surrounded him and the cart arrived. Campbell was loaded onto a backboard before the cart took him off the field.

Lions teammates took a knee and looked concerned as staff attended to him. Defensive end Aidan Hutchinsonwas in tears while the game was paused.

The Lions announced late Sunday night that Campbell was resting and was scheduled to remain in a local hospital overnight for continued evaluation and monitoring.

He was transported to a local hospital to be evaluated for a neck injury after exiting the team's Week 8 win over the Vikings.

Head coach Dan Campbell didn't have an update on the linebacker after the game.

"Thoughts and prayers are with Jack and his family," the coach said. "He's being taken care of. We don't have any new information."

JACK CAMPBELL: Lions All-Pro linebacker to remain in hospital after scary neck injury

Who is Jack Campbell?

Campbell is a linebacker for the Detroit Lions.

The 26-year-old is in his fourth NFL season, all with Detroit. The Lions drafted Campbell with the 18th overall pick in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft after he starred in college for the Iowa Hawkeyes.

A native of Cedar Falls, Iowa, Campbell broke out during his junior season with the Hawkeyes, totaling 143 tackles, two interceptions, two fumble recoveries and a sack in 2021. Returning for his senior season, Campbell was named an All-American in 2022 and received the Butkus Award as the top linebacker in college football.

He also received the William V. Campbell Trophy, also known as the "academic Heisman," in 2022 for being recognized as the college football player with the best combination of academics, leadership and on-field performance.

More: Jack Campbell is a Lions team captain. Here's why his teammates love him

Campbell slid right in as a key piece of the Lions' defense after arriving in the NFL. However, he didn't officially break out until his third season. Campbell recorded 176 total tackles, three forced fumbles and five sacks en route to being named a first-team All-Pro and earning his first Pro Bowl appearance last season.

On May 21, 2026, the Lions recognized Campbell's breakout with a four-year, $81 million extension.

Prior to his injury in Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season, Campbell hadn't missed a game in his four-year career.

item.title: KC Concepcion: Browns are confident, getting Shedeur Sanders ready for Sunday
item.description: The Browns haven't officially named Shedeur Sanders this week's starter, but with Deshaun Watson in the concussion protocol, all signs are pointing in that direction.
item.content:encoded:
The Browns haven't officially named Shedeur Sanders this week's starter, but with Deshaun Watson in the concussion protocol, all signs are pointing in that direction.

Those signs include Browns wide receiver KC Concepcion saying today that the offense is rallying around Sanders to get him ready to play against the Saints.

"It was unfortunate what happened to Deshaun, but we're going to pick up Shedeur's confidence, and get him ready for Sunday," Concepcion said.

Sanders lost a quarterback competition with Watson during the preseason, and Watson has played better than expected during the regular season. So Sanders has barely played this year, getting on the field just long enough to throw three passes. But on Sunday, he may start.

Last year Sanders started seven games as a rookie and struggled, but this year he'll get to show what kind of progress he's made. The Browns, who have playoff aspirations, have to hope he's ready.

item.title: Green Bay Packers News: Will the Packers be active at the trade deadline?
item.description: Do you think the Packers make a deal?
item.content:encoded:
We got one big early November Tuesday ordeal out of the way. Now the countdown is on for another one.

The annual “will they/won’t they” dance that precedes the NFL trade deadline every year is in full swing, with various speculators wondering who the Packers should target and what, if anything, they should give up to get them.

The Packers are still in the aftermath of their last big trade, of course, which affects what they could do at this year’s trade deadline. They seem unlikely to give up any serious assets in the 2027 NFL Draft considering they don’t have a first round pick.

But a lower-level trade might still be possible, especially if Gutekunst can get someone to bite on an offer involving 2028 assets.

Even so, as cap-strapped as the Packers are, it doesn’t seem super likely they’re going to be buyers at this year’s deadline. And there’s little the Packers could sell off, either. Keisean Nixon and Carrington Valentine are probably their two most notable assets on expiring (and thus very movable) contracts, and I don’t think the Packers are in a position to jettison either one, even if Valentine has fallen out of favor this year.

The safest bet seems like banking on this year being a quiet trade deadline. You’ll probably hear something about the Packers making calls or being in conversations, as always, but the chances of them landing a difference maker at the deadline seem low.

There is some positive news on the injury front for the Saints as they return from their bye week.

Rookie receiver Jordyn Tyson is set to return to practice on Wednesday, according to Nick Underhill of NewOrleans.football.

Tyson has been sidelined by a hamstring injury since training camp. He was placed on injured reserve with a designation to return when rosters were reduced to 53 players.

The Saints will have 21 days to activate Tyson to the 53-man roster.

The No. 8 overall pick of this year’s draft, Tyson should provide a boost to a team that is No. 14 in points scored and No. 23 in total yards.

The Saints will return to action at home against the Browns on Sunday.

item.title: Is Brandon Aiyuk coming back? WR applies for reinstatement, plans 49ers return
item.description: Brandon Aiyuk hasn't played an NFL game since the 2024 season. He is hoping to change that by applying for reinstatement. Here's what to know.
item.content:encoded:
Brandon Aiyuk hasn't played an NFL snap since Week 7 of the 2024 NFL season after tearing his ACL and becoming embroiled in a feud with the San Francisco 49ers.

It appears that Aiyuk is looking to change that as he takes the first step toward attempting a potential NFL comeback after his prolonged absence.

Aiyuk is officially applying for reinstatement to the NFL ahead of Week 9 of the 2026 season, ESPN's Adam Schefter reports. The 28-year-old's maneuver comes just days after news circulated that he had hired NFL agent Drew Rosenhaus to help lead his comeback bid.

Aiyuk had to apply for reinstatement because he has remained on the NFL's reserve/left team list since Dec. 13 of the 2025 season. Schefter reports Aiyuk is planning to report to the 49ers' facility on Friday, Nov. 6, at which point San Francisco will make a decision about his future.

So what does it mean for the receiver? And is a return to San Francisco a possibility? Here's what to know.

Is Brandon Aiyuk coming back?

Aiyuk will return to the NFL if he is reinstated. However, his return to the 49ers is a little less clear.

San Francisco will have to decide whether it wants to keep the receiver on the roster. If the team decides to move on, it can trade or release him. Once Aiyuk is reinstated, the team can't turn him away without a trade or release. Given the history between the two sides, it seems unlikely that Aiyuk would return to the 49ers' active roster.

49ers general manager John Lynch told reporters at a Jan. 21 press conference that Aiyuk had likely played his last snap for the team.

The team later took a stance that they would prefer to trade the receiver rather than grant his release.

"We're available. Give us a call," Lynch said of Aiyuk on April 26 after the 2026 NFL Draft. "And like I said earlier, I think it's the prudent thing to do. He’s an extremely talented player. He's been an extremely effective player in our league; situation didn't work itself out here. That's not to say that it can't be rekindled somewhere else. And we'd be happy to do something with anyone if the opportunity presented itself."

With Aiyuk potentially reporting to the team's facility on Friday, Nov. 6, it's unclear if that stance has changed.

In Nov. 2025, the Niners made the decision to void the guarantees in the receiver's contract after he "failed to attend meetings and declined to participate in other team activities," according to The Athletic. Aiyuk signed a four-year, $120 million extension in the 2024 offseason.

On the surface, Aiyuk returning could be a boost to a 49ers team that has no shortage of injuries at receiver. However, the bad blood between the two sides makes it likely that he'll have to continue his career with a different franchise.

Brandon Aiyuk stats

Here's a look at Aiyuk's stats since being drafted by the Niners in the first round of the 2020 NFL Draft:

  • 2020 (12 games): 60 catches (96 targets), 748 yards, five touchdowns; six carries, 77 rushing yards, two touchdowns
  • 2021 (17 games): 56 catches (84 targets), 826 yards, five touchdowns; five carries, 17 rushing yards
  • 2022 (17 games): 78 catches (114 targets), 1,015 yards, eight touchdowns; two carries, 23 rushing yards
  • 2023 (16 games): 75 catches (105 targets), 1,342 yards, seven touchdowns
  • 2024 (7 games): 25 catches (47 targets), 374 yards

item.title: Giants trade candidate: RB Derrick Henry
item.description: Could King Henry be the back the Giants need for a playoff push?
item.content:encoded:
Should the New York Giants, who are clearly big-game hunting in the running back market with the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline approaching, try to bring Derrick Henry to New York?

Head coach John Harbaugh has said he would love for the Giants to have a “Derrick Henry or Saquon Barkley situation” with the Giants. Clearly, Harbaugh does not believe Cam Skattebo gives him that.

The Baltimore Ravens’ season is falling apart. Baltimore is 4-4, last in the NFC North, and has lost its top two quarterbacks, Lamar Jackson (thumb) and Tyler Huntly (turf toe) for the season. The Ravens are going nowhere fast.

Mike Florio said on PFT Live that Henry should be begging for a trade to the Giants.

“If you’re Derrick Henry, are you showing up today and are you saying ‘Please trade me to the Giants’, or another contender … The season is going down the s——— for the Ravens right now. If I’m Henry and I’m looking at the calendar and I’m looking at the schedule and I’m looking at the situation and I’m thinking I’m not getting any younger and I’d kinda like to have a playoff run.

“If I’m the Giants and I’m looking at Jonathan Taylor if I’m John Harbaugh I’m calling my former GM Eric DeCosta today and I’m saying ‘is there any way that Derrick Henry could be available’.”

Why it would work

Henry, 6-foot-3, 252 pounds, has been one of the pre-eminent running backs in football for a decade. He was the lynchpin of Harbaugh’s rushing attacks with the Ravens the past two seasons, and is the model power/bellcow/explosive running back for a Harbaugh offense.

Henry is 32 with more than 3,000 touches in his career. That is a lot of mileage for a running back, and Henry is clearly past what is usually considered the expiration date for when backs are usually at their best. He gained more than 3,500 yards averaged more than 5 yards per carry the last two seasons with Harbaugh.

Henry is averaging a career-low 4.0 yards per carry this year. Is that about Henry? Jackson barely playing? A new offense with a team that has now lost three straight games?

Henry is in the final year of his contract. The Giants would be responsible only for the remaining pro-rated portions of his $11 million base salary and $1 million roster bonus. He has three void years in his contract, but the Ravens would be responsible for those as dead money.

As a rental, the Giants might not have to surrender as much draft capital for Henry as they would for Taylor.

Harbaugh has clearly shown a willingness to pick up the phone and try to broker deals. His relationships with DeCosta and Baltimore owner Steve Bisciotti might help get this one done.

Why it wouldn’t work

There are only two reasons I can think of. Maybe Henry really is finally slowing down. It would be up to Harbaugh and the Giants’ pro personnel department to make that decision. The other would be that the Giants might choose not to go the rental route.

item.title: Texans front office face a must-win game against the Chargers
item.description: Nick Caserio’s job is on the line and the Texans are about to break the huddle
item.content:encoded:
The Houston Texans face the only winless team in the NFL this Sunday when they take on the Los Angeles Chargers. Both teams had bigger plans that to waste away at the bottom of the AFC leaderboard

The Chargers season is toast. The Texans still have a glimmer of hope purely based on their history of digging themselves out of holes in the past. Plus, the AFC South is as winnable a division as there is this season.

The Texans lost their last three games by a combined 12 points. The Chargers have only scored above 20 points once this season, including scores of six, nine, and 14 twice.

For Houston, a win not only rights the ship and re-opens the opportunity to make a last-ditch effort to save the season, but its a mandatory performance for this coaching staff and front office. For all intents and purposes, a loss to the 0-7 LA Chargers will end the Nick Caserio era.

A 2-6 record with no early second round pick and a long list of undeveloped day two picks will be too much for this ownership group to look past. Houston has mortgaged their future without any near-term payout. They are $33.8M in the hole next year… before they even extend C.J. Stroud. Plus, they stand to lose Davis Mills, Tank Dell, Tommy Togiai, and Trent Brown. Houston is over-leveraged and is crashing like the ‘08 market.

One person not in the spotlight is Frank Edgerly the Senior Director of Football Research and Game Management. He’s been with the team since 2023 and is a disciple of Caserio stemming back from their time in New England. The Texans defensive scheme was observed, analyzed, and addressed by the entire league this offseason. His role in not addressing these issues by self-scouting has been apparent. Not to mention the game management issues late into the fourth quarter where the team has been our maneuvered time and time again.

The Chargers woes have stemmed from their horrific offensive line, inability to run the ball, and QB Justin Herbert’s regression. He’s thrown five touchdowns and 10 interceptions. When the Texans faced him in the 2024 AFC Wild Card Round, he had thrown just three interceptions all season. He’s been sacked 23 times on pace to pass his career high last year of 54. Houston desperately needs to add to both his interception and sack totals to win this do or die game against the Chargers.

On defense, the Chargers have struggled to generate pass rush all season. DEs Tuli Tuipulotu and Khalil Mack lead the team with three sacks each. Like Houston, they lack an inside pass rusher who can disrupt the pocket. Thats ideal for Houston, whose achilles heel has been conceding pressure on the inside. With a good pocket, C.J. Stroud should be able to find his top targets on offense.

Houston’s hot seat will remain hot even if Houston wins against the Chargers. They face next the Deshaun Watson-led Cleveland Browns, who are the darling of the 2026 season with a 5-3 record. Deshaun Watson’s trade, orchestrated by Nick Caserio in just his third month as General Manager. That trade netted Houston three first round picks, two fourth round pick, and a third.

Without the overwhelming draft capital he was able to use to maneuver throughout drafts, he has struggled to make sound decisions early in the draft. He’s reached on players to fill needs, creating further issues at critical positions such as offensive line and defensive tackle. The 2025 and 2026 draft classes have been rife with under-performing draft picks at high value selections. Caserio will be directly graded against the outcome of both this Chargers game Sunday and the upcoming matchup against Cleveland.

Both games are on the road.

All that being said, if Houston can turn it around these next two weeks, things do look up for them. They play the actively taking Colts, a Lamar Jackson-less Ravens team, a winnable game against the Steelers, and a tossup against the Commanders. If Houston exits this six-game stretch at 7-6, they will be squarely in the hunt for another wild card spot in a crowded AFC. 5-1 is mandatory for Houston. Otherwise they need to close up shop on this season and multiple members of the front office.

item.title: Eagles on pace for worst offense since 1998: How did it get to this point?
item.description: The Eagles have their worst offense through eight games this century. What were the factors that got them to this stage?
item.content:encoded:
There’s no argument the Philadelphia Eagles offense is bad. The 2026 unit is historically bad.

The Eagles are 29th in the NFL in points per game (17.1) and 30th in points per drive (1.61). They’re 32nd in yards per game (265.3) and yards per play (4.4), far from the offensive juggernauts the franchise has posted this century — whether that would be from Andy Reid, Chip Kelly, Doug Pederson, or even Nick Sirianni.

There has only been one Eagles team that has put up fewer points than the 2026 squad this century. The 2012 Eagles averaged just 16.6 points per game, and they ended up with a 4-12 record in what would be Reid’s last season. The 1.61 points per possession is also the lowest since 2012.

The 265.3 yards per game is the lowest through eight games since 1999 (244.0), and that Eagles team started 1-7 before rallying to finish 5-11 (year one under Reid). The 4.42 yards per play is the lowest since 1999 (3.92), and only the 1998 offense was worse than those two (3.73).

Those 1998 Eagles were an abomination. They were 30th out of 30 teams in points per game (10.1) and yards per game (261.7). That was the only time in franchise history the Eagles finished in the 30s in points and yards per game. If points per possession and yards per possession were measured in 1998, the Eagles would have been last in those categories too.

The 2026 Eagles have the worst offense this century, and is the worst Eagles offense since 1998. That unit had Bobby Hoying start the seaosn before a rotating carousel of quarterbacks that included Rodney Peete and Koy Detmer. The Eagles went from Hoying to Peete before returning to Hoying and eventually Detmer.

So how did the 2026 Eagles get to this point? How did they go from a top-10 offense, to middle of the back, to what they are now — all over the past year?

There were quite a few contributing factors towards the Eagles offense reaching historically bad levels for the franchise.

1. Jeff Stoutland deciding not to return

The Eagles offensive line was middle of the pack last season, the first time in the Nick Sirianni era the offensive line wasn’t a top-10 unit. Outside of Lane Johnson, all the other starters on the offensive line started 14+ games — so injuries didn’t play a factor in the mediocrity.

Stoutland’s role as run-game coordinator also regressed, as Nick Sirianni and former offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo began incorporating different run designs to the offense. With these changes in place, Stoutland reportedly wasn’t consulted about them as his title was in name only.

With Stoutland not having a prominent voice as in years past, he decided to step aside after the 2025 season. Chris Kuper was hired as the offensive line coach, despite the Minnesota Vikings ranking 31st in sack rate (11.0%) and 27th in pressure rate allowed per dropback (39.8%) last season. The Vikings were 26th in sack rate (8.0%) and 29th in pressure rate (37.8%) from 2022 to 2025 under Kuper.

The Eagles offensive line under Kuper this year? They are 24th in sack rate (7.9%) and 28th in pressure rate (42.7%). They were 19th in sack rate (6.7%) and 20th in pressure rate (35.4%) last year.

2. The Kevin Patullo hire, followed by Sean Mannion hire

The Eagles were coming off a Super Bowl victory in the 2024 season, but offensive coordinator Kellen Moore was leaving after one season to take the New Orleans Saints head coaching job. Philadelphia didn’t have a deep opol of candidates for the offensive coordinator role since the Eagles played into February, so Patullo was promoted from passing game coordinator to offensive coordinator.

Patullo was passing game coordinator for four seasons, and came over from the Indianapolis Colts with Nick Sirianni. His lone season as offensive coordinator was a disaster, as the scoring dropped from 27.2 points per game to 22.3 (seventh to 19th) and points per possession from 2.50 to 2.00 (eighth to 21st). Yards per game dropped from 367.2 to 3111.2 (seventh to 24th) and yards per play from 5.6 to 5.2 (11th to 19th). The Eagles went from 24.7% in three-and-out rate to 36.0% (21st to fourth).

The offense got worse with Sean Mannion hired to replace Patullo, as the changes to the offensive scheme has made the unit worst. Injuries to the offense haven’t helped (Jordan Mailata is the only player to start every game), but the Eagles are historically bad on offense.

To showcase Mannion’s struggles, look at the second half of games.The Eagles average 4.6 points per game and 3.9 yards per play (both 32nd in the NFL). The third quarter is even worse, ranking 32nd in points per game (1.6), yards per game (43.0), yards per carry (2.5), yards per play (3.1), and yards per attempt (4.0).

The offense went from bad to worse.

3. Lane Johnson retiring

Johnson’s sudden retirement played a factor in how this offense has performed, as the Eagles haven’t won a game since his sudden retirement after Week 4. The Eagles are 0-3 since Johnson retired, and 3-8 in games he’s missed since last season (including playoffs).

The Eagles were 122-63-1 with Johnson in the lineup, a .659 win percentage (including postseason). They are 18-30 without him, a .375 win percentage.

Johnson’s replacement at right tackle, Markel Bell, has had a rough start to his career. Bell has allowed five sacks in his three starts, and is tied for second amongst right tackles in most sacks allowed. He has allowed a 7.3% pressure rate per dropback this season — seventh-worst amongst right tackles in the NFL.

Right tackle is a new position for Bell, and he wasn’t expected to play this year. Bell was expected to take over for Johnson after this season, just three years after moving up to FBS from Holmes Community College.

The Eagles were going to have to adjust to life without Johnson at some point. This wasn’t expected to happen this season.

4. Jalen Hurts out for the season

Any time a team loses their franchise quarterback hurts. What Jalen Hurts over the past month is way bigge rthan football.

Hurts was discovered to have a having a superficial blood clot in his leg following the team’s trip to London, which was discovered before he played in the team’s Week 5 game against the Jaguars. An ultrasound in the middle of that week found the blood clot had moved to his lungs, which put Hurts on blood thinners and ruled him out for the season.

The Eagles are 58-25 in games Hurts has started since he became the full-time starting quarterback in 2021, a .699 win percentage. Without Hurts, the Eagles are 3-7 in 10 games — a .300 win percentage.

The Eagles passing game has struggled with Hurts, but he has found ways to win football games. They just aren’t getting that when Hurts isn’t on the field.

In the three games Tanner McKee has started, the Eagles are 32nd in yards per play (4.2), 31st in yards per attempt (5.6), and 29th in offensive points per game (15.0). McKee has completed 63.2% of his passes for 638 yards with 2 TD, 2 INT, and a 76.6 passer rating. He is 31st out of 32 qualified quarterbacks in yards per attempt (5.6) and 26th in passer rating.

There is a massive drop off from Hurts to McKee, who couldn’t beat out Andy Dalton for the QB2 job this summer.

5. Failure to address TE position

The Eagles didn’t have the depth at tight end in the 2025 season, despite Dallas Goedert having 11 touchdown catches. Goedert had 591 receiving yards and the rest of the tight ends had a combined 116. While the Eagles ranked 22nd in tight end receiving yards, they also had a significant hole in blocking at the position.

The Eagles addressed the position by signing Johnny Mundt to a one-year contract as the blocking tight end and drafting Eli Stowers in the second round to be the TE2 behind Goedert. Stowers struggled to gain separation from defenders in minicamp, which moved over to training camp before missing the first six games with hamstring and quad injuries.

Mundt has struggled as a blocker while being the de facto TE2. A Grant Calcaterra injury at the end of training camp didn’t help matters either. Once Goedert missed time with a knee injury, the Eagles had to sign 36-year-old Zach Ertz just to have a pass catcher at the position.

Ertz can’t get elevated to the active roster, Mundt is struggling in the offense, and Stowers has just two games into his career. Stowers had 46 yards in garbage time in Sunday’s loss to Washington, placing him second on the team in receiving yards for the tight end position.

Goedert has 258 receiving yards and the reminder of the Eagles tight ends have a combined 91. The Eagles are 17th in the NFL in receiving yards amongst tight ends with 349, but also haven’t had their bye week yet.

While the position is healthy now, Mannion’s offense thrives with two and three tight ends on the field. The Eagles have one capable tight end at this point, which is on the front office for not addressing the position well enough in the offseason.

Perhaps more playing time for Stowers will change that, even if the only time he’s been effective is late in games when the outcome has bene determined.

item.title: Was this a 1-game demotion for Ashton Jeanty?
item.description: How did Raiders’ 2nd-year players fare in Week 8?
item.content:encoded:
Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 38-33 win at the New York Jets on Sunday and what to look for Sunday at the San Francisco 49ers.

Ashton Jeanty:

The No. 6 overall draft pick saw his play time and work load decrease dramatically. He played a career low 40 percent of the snaps, but more importantly, the Boise State product had just two carries as he saw rookie fourth-round pick Mike Washington get a whopping 25 carries. Raiders coach Klint Kubiak said the decision had nothing to so with Jeanty’s disparaging words about the Jets’ defense. We will see if Jeanty gets more work against the 49ers. But this was a major development.

Jack Bech:

The second-round pick returned from spending four games on the injured reserve with a broken forearm. He played 40 percent of the snaps, but was not targeted as a wide receiver.

Darien Porter:

The third-round pick injured his groin on the first play from scrimmage. His availability for Sunday’s game is unknown.

Caleb Rogers:

The third-round pick was benched after he started two games at right guard, in favor of rookie Trey Zuhn. Kubiak indicated Zuhn will play against the 49ers. Rogers played two plays on offense and six on special teams.

Charles Grant:

The offensive lineman, taken in the third round, didn’t play on offense as usual, but he did log five snaps on special teams.

Dont’e Thornton:

The wide receiver, taken in the fourth round, was activated from the injured reserve, but he was a healthy scratch. So, that’s not overly encouraging.

Tonka Hemingway:

The fourth-round pick suffered a stinger for the second time since Week 5. His availability for Sunday in unknown.

JJ Pegues:

The defensive tackle, taken in the sixth round, was inactive for the fifth time this season. It was a bit of a surprise since he had a forced fumble in Week 7 and the team had just waived Jonah Laulu. Meanwhile, rookie Tim Keenan, elevated from the practice squad, has been getting quality playing time the past two weeks. It leads to speculation that a Keenan-for-Pegues roster move could potentially be in play at some point.

Cody Lindenberg:

The seventh-round pick played 18 snaps on special teams, which is his norm. He didn’t play on defense, a week after he had three defensive snaps, his first defensive action of his career.

item.title: Brian Schottenheimer report card: Out-coached again in another loss
item.description: This has been a bad week for Brian Schottenheimer.
item.content:encoded:
Do you remember when you were a kid and your parents always hounded you about how much better of a student you would be if you just applied yourself? No… just me?

Well, for what feels like the 100th time this season, Brian Schottenheimer brought home a failing report card to his disappointed parents, and his lack of ability to properly understand how to attack his opponent based on tape is very concerning.

Even after putting up 30 points in the Cowboys 33-30 loss, Schottenheimer (along with Christian Parker) was the clear problem for the Cowboys. Whether it’s failed challenges, ultra-conservativeness, questionable fourth-down play calls, extreme lack of creativity, or the stubbornness to establish the run, the Cowboys offense is consistently put on hard-mode week in-and-week out.

The first half was filled with inefficient runs, setting the Cowboys up behind the chains and trying to convert on third-and-longs way too much. After torching the Philadelphia Eagles on the ground in week seven, the Cowboys were dedicated to replicating their running game success against the Cardinals, and they finished the game with 39 carriers for 93 yards (2.4 yards per carry).

With the running game hurting them a ton in this game, the Cowboys relied on Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, and Ryan Flournoy to carry the load. The only problem was the passing concepts looked eerily similar to how it did in Weeks 1-6. Very little motion, few bunch sets, and basic, static route concepts that make things extremely difficult for anyone to create separation in the passing game.

With the run game setting them back, and the lack of modern day passing concepts making things very easy to defend, the Cowboys found themselves stalling out in the second half and blowing a two-possession lead with just four minutes to go in the game.

The main concern with Schottenheimer (outside of everything else we’ve already touched on) is his inability to close games out as a play-caller. For his entire tenure at the head coach and play-caller for the Cowboys, Schottenheimer has called the game was too passive. His inability to understand how poor his defense has been for a year-and-a-half now has cost this football team wins.

For a coach who has a $60-million dollar quarterback, two highly paid wide receivers, and an offensive line loaded with highly paid players and first-round picks, Schottenheimer puts more faith in his defense and special teams than he does his talented and highly-paid offense.

The end of the first half field goal attempt was the first of many signs of this throughout the game. With 11-seconds left in the first half and a timeout in his back pocket, Schottenheimer elected to run the football for a minimal gain and send out Brandon Aubrey for a 61-yard field goal attempt.

Aubrey, who has struggled mightily with the longer field goal attempts so far this season, missed the field goal, and the Cowboys carried a 14-3 game into half. Why not try to gain 10-15 yards with a timeout in your back pocket and the entire field at your disposal?

The next drive that had a heavy weight on his grade was the Cowboys second to last drive in the fourth quarter. With the ball on the Cardinals 20-yard line up three points, the Cowboys ran Javonte Williams up the middle for no gain to get the Cardinals to burn their last time out, which was the right call.

The next play call perfectly encases all of Schottenheimer’s warts as a play-caller. With the two-minute warning looming, the Cowboys were in a perfect position to go for the jugular. Instead, with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens standing on the sideline, Schottenheimer dialed up a slow developing play-action pass with everyone on the field and in the stadium knowing the Cowboys should and would be passing.

The result? An L.J. Collier sack losing six yards. On 3rd-and-16, Schottenheimer did what he often does in less than ideal down and distances, runs Williams straight into a brickwall for a minimal gain. Brandon Aubrey came on to give the Cowboys a six-point lead with a minute to go and no timeouts for the Cardinals. In most instances, that’s enough to win the football game, but the Cowboys defense had other plans, as they often have in 2026.

The decision to run play-action with Lamb and Pickens on the sideline, with a chance to ice the game was absolutely mind-boggling. Schottenheimer commented on his choice of personnel, pointing to a similar package earlier in the game on the Ryan Flournoy touchdown pass in the second quarter.

I would certainly hope Schottenheimer understands the difference between a 3rd-and-1 in the first quarter of a 7-0 game and potentially the last play from scrimmage when the defense is forced to play aggressive to create negative plays from the offense, but who really knows right now.

Play-Calling

F

Fourth-Down Decisions

C

I loved Schottenheimer’s decision to go for the fourth down on the opening drive of the game, but absolutely hated the play call and formation that got stuffed.

Timeout Usage

F

Team Preparation

F

It was all pretty ugly, yet again.

What grade would you give to Brian Schottenheimer on Sunday?

item.title: Seahawks Reacts Survey: Is Sam Darnold Seattle’s starting quarterback in 2027?
item.description: What does the future hold at quarterback for the Seattle Seahawks?
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country.

It’s crazy to be talking about an important part of a Super Bowl champion being off the team completely just a short time later, but we might be at that point with Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold. The NFC Championship Game brilliance seems like a distant memory given the horror show to start the 2026 season. Seattle’s offensive woes are not exclusively Darnold’s fault, but he certainly has a helping hand in this mess.

We aren’t running another poll on benching Darnold this season. Heck, if Drew Lock is going to remain sidelined with his elbow injury, then you can shelve any fantasy about giving Lock any run. But we’re absolutely at the point where barring an amazing second half of the season, Darnold’s future as Seahawks starter should be called into question. The franchise QB he looked like for about 10 weeks last year and the playoff run has regressed back to something close to the worst version of himself, and that volatility doesn’t sound like a recipe for a massive contract extension. Darnold’s contract is up in 2027, so he could play out the rest of his deal and have another “prove-it” moment, possibly with a different offensive coordinator (again). Alternatively, John Schneider pivots and starts looking for his next guy, whether that’s believing in Year 3 Jalen Milroe, re-signing Lock to essentially recreate the Darnold magic with someone else, trading for a quarterback, or drafting one.

item.title: Chicago Bears Pass Protection Analysis on the Sack Allowed vs Seahawks
item.description: Given the opponent and environment, the Bears had one of their better pass-protection days against the Seahawks. @wiltfongjr breaks it down here.
item.content:encoded:
In the first two games since Caleb Williams returned, the Chicago Bears’ pass protection allowed 4 sacks to the Atlanta Falcons and then 3 to the New England Patriots. It’s not bad, and in context, I thought the pass protection was solid in each game, but it was still a much higher sack rate than a season ago, when he averaged just 1.4 per game.

The Seattle Seahawks defense featured 5 players with multiple sacks through their first seven games, and with the Week 8 matchup in loud Lumen Field in Seattle, I figured their defense would get the best of Chicago’s pass protection scheme a few times.

But the Bears only allowed 1 sack to Seattle’s vaunted defense, and I’ll break it down right here.

  • Sack 19: 4th Quarter: 2-10-CHI 23 (14:02) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at CHI 13 for -10 yards (M.Morris)

After Caleb faked to D’Andre Swift, he looked downfield at Luther Burden III (outside the right hash), but he felt pressure off the left so fast because left tackle Theo Benedet was walked back into the pocket. Caleb drifted right and looked to Swift in the left flat, but didn’t have a clear throwing lane. Benedet did a nice job staying between his guy and his quarterback, but the problem was the depth he gave up, so even though his guy didn’t get the sack, he’s the reason this play was blown up.

If Benedet offered up just a bit more resistance, Williams could have hit one of his three checkdowns (probably Colston Loveland over the middle), but there wasn’t time to get through his progressions.

It looked like Swift was going to chip if Benedet’s guy took an outside rush. He got a small piece of the defender on the way to the flat, but with the Seattle rush end square to Benedet, there wasn’t enough for Swift to hit

Benedet set up inside first, then kicked out for the edge defender. In theory, that inside step would normally entice a defender to go around the edge, exposing his outside shoulder for Swift to target on his chip release and leaving Benedet in a good position as the defender redirected his rush inside. But the Seattle defender had his mind made up to bull rush on the play. Benedet likely didn’t expect it and was driven back.

Caleb was forced out of the pocket and ended up even with left guard Joe Thuney, who pulled right to block the edge after a Loveland release. Mike Morris (#94) just reached out and grabbed Williams before delivering the belly-to-back suplex.

The Bears did a good job mixing up the tempo and identifying the Seattle defenders all night long, which is hard to do

To turn the page from Week 8 to Week 9, I spent some time early this week watching the Miami Dolphins’ most recent game to see what’s in store for the Detroit Lions.

Here are my five Lions vs. Dolphins thoughts after watching Miami’s 24-19 loss to the New England Patriots.

Note: It’s worth mentioning that it was a very rainy day in Miami, particularly at the start and end of the game.

Malik Willis holds onto the ball for a loooooong time

There could be a lot of reasons for it, but Willis holds onto the ball way too long in the pocket. Per NFL Pro, Willis’ 3.05 average seconds to throw is third-longest in the league. Is it taking Willis too long to go through his progressions, is he too hesitant to trust his eyes, or is his young receiving corps just not getting open? It’s hard to say from my vantage point, but it certainly is an opportunity for the Lions to get home against Willis.

Thus far, Willis has taken 21 sacks—the seventh most in the NFL—and the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate in the NFL (10.3%).

The Patriots got to Willis five times in the first half, before backing down a little in the second.

This could be a big Tyleik Williams game

Miami had an extremely hard time stopping Patriots nose tackle Cory Durden in this game. He set career highs in pressure (three), quarterback hits (three), and sacks (1.5). Prior to this game, Durden had never recorded a sack and only had two quarterback hits since starting his NFL career, coincidentally in Detroit, in 2023.

Miami is particularly vulnerable on the right side of the line, where second-year right guard Jonah Savaiinaea is the 66th (out of 75) PFF-graded guard (47.9), and right tackle Austin Jackson is the lowest-graded tackle in football (44.6).

Williams is having a strong start to his second season, remaining a force in the run game (Dolphins rank 21st in EPA/rush, 24th in success rate) while growing as a pass rusher. Obviously, look out for Alim McNeill, too, who is currently only behind Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen in PFF pressures from interior defenders (31).

The Lions’ run game should find success

Last week, the Lions found success pounding the rock right up the middle of the Vikings’ defense. That should be the game plan once again against the Dolphins. Rhamondre Stevenson toughed out 82 yards on 19 carries (4.3 YPC), as the Patriots produced a 45.2% success rate on the ground—ninth-highest of all Week 8 performances.

For the year, Miami ranks 21st in EPA/rush allowed and 30th in success rate (43.9%).

So they aren’t giving up a ton of explosive plays on the ground, but you can certainly grind them down. I would not be surprised to see another solid workload from Sione Vaki.

But Miami does have some dudes on defense

Miami’s defense as a whole won’t likely be up for the task against the Lions’ high-flying offense. The Dolphins rank 24th in points per game allowed (25.9) and 25th in yards per play allowed.

However, there are a couple of players who are playing well and capable of game-changing plays. The first is edge rusher Josh Uche. While Uche only has two sacks this year (one against the Patriots), he’s produced PFF’s ninth-highest run defense grade among edge defenders (76.0).

On the next level, rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez flashed against the Patriots. He had a teach-tape punchout and was second on the team with eight tackles. His rookie season has seen some ups and downs, but don’t be surprised if he makes a big play or two against the Lions.

The game wasn’t as close as the score

While the Dolphins only lost by five and they held a 10-point lead at halftime, this game did not feel like it was truly competitive between the teams.

For one, the Patriots made a ton of mistakes in the first half. They fumbled inside their own red zone, missed a 40-yard field goal, and had a ton of untimely penalties (seven in total). In the second half, the Patriots dropped an easy interception, and they had a game-clinching pick erased by an away-from-the-play offsides penalty.

And the Dolphins only made it close thanks to a prevent-defense touchdown with just over two minutes, because a Patriots defender fell down for an easy 35-yard touchdown.

On a per play basis, the Patriots produced more yards per play (5.3 vs. 4.5), and had a much higher success rate (49.1% vs. 43.8%). If you take away garbage-time stats, the difference is even bigger in success rate (52.9% vs. 39.3%).

If the Lions can avoid making self-inflicted mistakes, they should be able to win comfortably, despite the fact that Miami has kept each of their last four games within a touchdown.

item.title: NFL Injury Report, Week 9: Latest news, updates on Bhayshul Tuten, Breece Hall, more players for fantasy football
item.description: We go over the NFL injury report going into Week 9, with player updates, news and fantasy football analysis.
item.content:encoded:
Week 9 is the official midway point of the 2026 NFL season. So by now you know what you have on your fantasy football roster. You also know who has been healthy the majority of the year and which players have missed time. It feels like the injury report is thinning out a bit as we get into the middle of the campaign. But as always, we're tracking all the latest news and updates for you, to help with those fantasy football lineups.

NFL Injury Report, Week 9

Quarterback

  • Lamar Jackson, BAL (thumb) — Will be placed on injured reserve

  • Tyler Huntley, BAL (toe) — Reportedly done for the season

  • Kyler Murray, MIN (hamstring)

  • Matthew Stafford, LAR (arm)

Ravens QBs: Jackson left in the first half of Sunday's loss to the Bills. He needs surgery on his thumb and is headed for IR. He'll miss at least four games, if not the rest of the season. After Jackson exited, Huntley entered the game and also had to leave due to injury (turf toe), which will end his season. That leaves Baltimore down to third-string rookie Joe Fagnano, who will start against Jacksonville on TNF. Hayden Winks takes a closer look at what Fagnano could bring.

The QB instability is obviously a huge downgrade to the passing game. Fagnano went 10 of 21 for 91 yards and an INT in his first NFL action in Week 8. Zay Flowers is more of a WR3/flex option while Derrick Henry should get a healthy amount of work, though in a tough matchup. Outside of those two, the rest of the Ravens offense should be avoided in fantasy until we see more from Fagnano or the Ravens make a deal for a QB.

Running Back

  • Christian McCaffrey, SF (hamstring)

  • Bhayshul Tuten, JAX (ankle/foot) — Game-time decision

  • Jeremiyah Love, ARI (ankle) — Will be placed on IR, miss 4-5 weeks

  • Bam Knight, ARI (concussion)

  • Cam Skattebo, NYG (hamstring)

  • Breece Hall, NYJ (quad) — Expected to be back in Week 9

  • Kyle Monangai, CHI (toe/thumb)

  • David Montgomery, HOU (groin)

  • Travis Etienne Jr., NO (hamstring) — Could be activated off IR

  • TreVeyon Henderson, NE (illness)

  • Brian Robinson Jr., ATL (hamstring)

Tuten: Jaguars coach Liam Coen said the running back will be a game-time decision for Thursday’s game agains the Ravens. Tuten was a DNP Monday and Tuesday, but is expected to get some type of work in Wednesday. He is coming off the best game of the season. He took 18 touches for 159 yards and two scores in Week 8. Chris Rodriguez Jr. is also dealing with a hand injury but was limited on Monday and Tuesday.

If Tuten is out, Rodriguez gets elevated into the RB2/3 conversation given the Jags are a 10-point favorite. In the rout of the Colts last week, Rodriguez had 58 yards on seven touches and a score. Ameer Abdullah also saw six carries against Indy and could see some work if Tuten is sidelined.

Hall: We thought the Jets were going to get back Hall in Week 8 against the Raiders. That wasn't the case and we got another solid game from Braelon Allen. At this point, even if Hall comes back, expect Allen to be involved given how well he's performed. Allen is the RB5 overall in half-PPR scoring from Weeks 5-8 with Hall sidelined. We'll need to get a look at how the split is in Week 9 with Hall back. Plus, it's a tough draw against Kansas City's run defense. But better matchups loom, so don't be surprised if both Hall and Allen are viable RB2/3 options.

Cardinals RBs: Love suffered a new high-ankle sprain in the comeback win over Dallas in OT on Sunday. Knight exited after a big hit and should land in concussion protocol. It'll be tough for Knight to clear in time for Week 9 against the Seahawks, but we'll see. Love has had so many issues with the ankle in his rookie season, and is expected to miss 4-5 weeks while on injured reserve, per NFL Network's Ian Rapoport. With Love already out, if Knight sits, Tyler Allgeier will be playable, but don't expect 33.6 fantasy points — or anywhere close to that — against Seattle's top defense.

But with Love on IR and Knight starting the season with a lesser role, expect Allgeier to be the lead back moving forward. There could be weeks when Knight is healthy in which the staff rides the hot hand. But Allgeier was brought in to be a high-value backup to Love. Allgeier will have RB2/3 value week-to-week depending on the matchup. Also keep an eye our for James Conner, who is on IR but could be a useful stash.

McCaffrey: CMC comes off the bye navigating a mild hamstring strain. It doesn't feel like this will cause him to miss Week 9 against the Raiders. But we saw before San Francisco's bye that Kyle Shanahan feels comfortable giving the ball to rookie Kaelon Black. We could see more of Black on Sunday to help keep McCaffrey fresh.

Wide Receiver

  • Christian Watson, GB (ribs)

  • Jakobi Meyers, JAX (hamstring/ankle)

  • DeVonta Smith, PHI (hamstring)

  • Michael Wilson, ARI (ribs)

  • Mike Evans, SF (Achilles)

  • A.J. Brown, NE (ankle/knee)

  • Emeka Egbuka, TB (foot) — Could play in Week 9

  • Jordyn Tyson, NO (hamstring) — Could come off IR

  • Deebo Samuel Sr., SF (hamstring)

Watson: The Packers' lead receiver had a miraculous exit and return to TNF's win over the Panthers in Week 8. Watson finished with an 8-113-0 line on 10 targets, catching a few passes after coming back from the hospital. But Watson revealed he's dealing with a broken rib, which is less than ideal. He'll have ample time to rest before Week 9's matchup with the Patriots. Watson could play through the injury, but if he's active, he would be at risk of exiting the game early. If Watson ends up having to sit, Tucker Kraft and Savion Williams would likely see more targets. Matthew Golden would be elevated into WR1 territory as well.

Wilson: The Cardinals' receiver told reporters after Sunday's win over the Cowboys that he's dealing with broken ribs. It appears Wilson is going to play through the injury. He's a risky option in the flex in PPR formats going up against the Seahawks' stout defense in Week 9.

Egbuka: The Bucs wideout has missed the past two games, and Tampa's passing game sure could use him. The Bucs didn't complete a pass in Week 8's shutout win over the Falcons, instead opting to run the ball 56 times for 324 yards. That likely won't be the case in Chicago in Week 9. If Egbuka can get back, it's a decent matchup, though Tampa Bay ranks dead last in passing offense this season. Egbuka would be a risky flex at best.

Tight End

  • Hunter Henry, NE (foot)

  • Jake Ferguson, DAL (ankle)

  • Colby Parkinson, LAR (ribs)

Ferguson: The Cowboys lost Ferguson to a low-ankle sprain early in the game against Arizona. He didn't return and his status for Week 9 against the Colts could be up in the air. If Ferguson is out, this is still a passing game dominated by CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens. Ryan Flournoy has stepped up as a solid WR3 as well. Brevyn Ford-Spann played 88% of the snaps in Week 8 and had four catches on five targets for 31 yards. In deeper formats, Ford-Spann isn't a bad streamer. He could see garbage-time looks if the Cowboys run away against a struggling Indy team.

item.content:encoded:
The Pittsburgh Steelers are enjoying their bye week and 6-2 record. Pittsburgh’s defense has been the star of the show this season and has continued to trend in the right direction. The defensive line is ferocious, and the defense is filled with veterans and young stars. The trade of Joey Porter, Jr. looks better with each game as Daylen Everette has been excellent at cornerback.

Speaking of the coverage, what coverages has Pittsburgh leaned into in 2026? Pittsburgh is a zone coverage defense with 35.3% of coverages in Cover 3 and 23.7% in Cover 4. Cover 2 is run 14.2% of the time, with Cover 6 having the lowest total at 9.5%.

The man coverages played for Pittsburgh are Cover 1 Man at 9.1%, Cover 0 at 4.4%, and Cover 2 Man at 0.3%. The total EPA allowed per dropback is the sixth best in the NFL at -0.02.
