item.title: Brian Thomas Jr. to the Patriots, Jonathan Taylor to the Vikings and more trades we'd love to see for fantasy football
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Chris Allen plays armchair GM ahead of the 2026 NFL Trade Deadline.
item.content:encoded:
Think about how much work goes into a fantasy football trade. We plug offers into trade analyzers. We scroll through other leagues' deals looking for a framework that might fit. We go back and forth with the other manager for days. And even after we hit accept, there's a little voice wondering if the league chat is about to roast us.

Now imagine doing that as an actual NFL GM.

Salary caps. Draft capital. A fan base and a local media market ready to grade every move before the ink dries. I'll stick with my group chat, thanks.

Luckily, we don't have to worry about any of that today. With the NFL Trade Deadline next Tuesday and after playing couch coach on Sunday, let's sit back and play armchair GM. No cap sheets, no press conferences. Just the deals that would make our fantasy lives a little easier. Here are five trades I'd love to see before the deadline.

Brian Thomas Jr. to the Patriots

All right, let me inject some reality into the situation as you scoff at my idea. The odds of the Jaguars helping to improve a team in the same conference with a 71% shot at the playoffs are about as good as me getting more than five wins in the Yahoo Expert League. But Jacksonville has at least been having fun with giving credence to letting one of their young WRs go via trade.

Brian Thomas Jr. starts the scoring in Jacksonville!

INDvsJAX on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/TSkI5R33VG

— NFL (@NFL) November 1, 2026

I'm putting the following two bits of information in the "probably (definitely) doesn't matter" category. First, the Jaguars' 'Weapons'-themed Halloween post. All of the primary skill players got a space on the poster — even LeQuint Allen Jr. Everyone but Brian Thomas Jr. But then, the third-year WR co-led the Jaguars in targets on Sunday before the game got out of hand. 

(Windhorst fingers) Why would Jacksonville do that?

But seriously, Thomas' decline since '24 has been due to his fit within the offense. Trevor Lawrence is targeting the middle of the field at the sixth-highest rate of all starters. Through eight weeks, Thomas has three targets on patterns over the middle. The same problem existed last year, too (6 of 48 catches on crossing routes). Thomas' superpower has been downfield and outside the numbers. In '25, he had the same amount of yards as Parker Washington on throws of 15 or more air yards. Jacksonville has plenty of (better) options for Lawrence. New England could use at least another.

#Patriots QB Drake Maye absolutely launched the post on the Kyle Williams touchdown after sliding up to avoid pressure. Air distance of 46.9 yards. Wish we had the MPH. pic.twitter.com/XFMPJF4OKO

— Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) November 2, 2026

Since the schedule opened up for the Patriots in Week 4, Drake Maye is averaging 9.1 air yards per attempt. Only Jordan Love is throwing farther. But despite throwing to Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas and Efton Chism, Maye is fourth in completion rate on downfield throws. Romeo Doubs is out until at least Week 12, Hunter Henry sustained a foot injury on Sunday and A.J. Brown's ankle and knee injuries have made him more of a liability than an asset. The schedule won't shield them from tough defenses forever. If they want to make another run at the Super Bowl, they'll need another receiver to keep the offense on schedule.

Josh Downs to the Bengals

Please tell me you're not surprised that I'd want a Josh-Downs-caliber WR in orange and black. Admittedly, Downs looked like he went to the Cam Newton School of Fumble Recoveries on Sunday. But a southeastern, 110-mile change of scenery would do him some good. Besides, his utility to a passing attack like the Bengals' is easy to see.

How do you think Josh Downs could potentially fit in the Steelers offense? pic.twitter.com/sk62DD8dPQ

— PorterLessBurgh (@PortersBurgh) October 28, 2026

Downs has lined up in the slot on 54.5% of his snaps with an aDOT of 9.3 air yards. Daniel Jones' avg. time to throw on passes to Downs has been 2.55 seconds. Joe Burrow has been firing the ball at 2.57 seconds post-snap and targeting the intermediate area of the field (11th in air yards per att.). On third down alone, Downs' 13 catches have resulted in series conversions. But adding Indy's slot guy isn't just about how he helps No. 9. He'd also put No. 1 in better situations.

  • (Ja'Marr Chase) Yards per Route Run: 2.30 (from the outside), 1.45 (from the slot)

  • First Downs per Route Run: 11.6%, 7.7%

  • Explosive Play Rate: 20.9%, 16.7%

Chase's TD against the Titans started with him from the perimeter. In fact, all of his touchdown catches have come from the outside. While we enjoy the layup looks, Chase has been more efficient when taking on boundary coverage. And if Cincinnati can add a reliable slot receiver to the mix, its offense will add a much-needed element to their passing game.

Jonathan Taylor to the Vikings

I'll eat the chalk on Jonathan Taylor heading north. It's in the same vein as the Bengals adding to their receiver corps. The strength of Minnesota's offense isn't through Kyler Murray. That (Viking) ship has sailed. But, for as much blame as we should lay at his feet, Murray still needed an average of 8.2 yards on his 10 third-down dropbacks. And some of that stems from the help, or lack thereof, he got from the running game.

Here are all nine Jordan Mason carries against Detroit.

Gaints of 10, 1, -2, 2, 29 (called back), 11, -5, 2, 1

What stands out? pic.twitter.com/2VmLUUm3Q2

— Will Ragatz (@WillRagatz) November 2, 2026

To be honest, I don't disagree with Will Ragatz's (perceived) sentiment. I'm not sure what more Jordan Mason could do on his early-down opportunities. But when six of eight totes go for two or fewer yards, explanations matter less. And let's say Taylor gets a chance to run behind the same offensive line. At least from looking at his per-touch metrics to date, there's a solid chance he'd get a bit more on his touches.

  • Adj. Yards After Contact per Att. (on early downs): 3.42 (Taylor), 2.65 (Mason)

  • Rushing Success Rate: 38.7%, 34.8%

  • Forced Missed Tackle Rate: 12.1%, 17.4%

Outside of making a couple of extra guys miss, Mason has been as advertised: good, just needs volume. Meanwhile, before the Colts put a "For Sale" sign outside of Lucas Oil Stadium, Taylor was one of eight RBs with more than 500 rushing yards on early downs. Accordingly, Jones' average distance to the sticks on third down was 7.3 yards.

Maybe HC Kevin O'Connell has some magic left in his playcalling to get Murray comfortable. But the defense can still cause havoc, and a better run game can take pressure off Murray. And if the price is as steep as the reports indicate, Minnesota wouldn't be crazy for paying it.

George Pickens to the Seahawks

I wasn't hip to the idea of George Pickens leaving Dallas until a few things happened within a span of about 24 hours. The first two went down this past Sunday. 

George Pickens running to the locker room before the game is over in Dallas. 👀 #Steelers#NFLpic.twitter.com/Z1QRLzHat9

— Blitzburgh (@Blitz_Burgh) November 2, 2026

Seeing Pickens already halfway to his car before the Cardinals kicked the winning FG should also go in the "probably (definitely) doesn't matter" bucket. It's not his first negative reaction to a loss. However, couple that with a usage shift over his last few games, and there might be more to the story.

  • Target Share: 19% (Weeks 6-8), 24% (Weeks 1-3)

  • Air Yard Share: 26%, 33%

  • Play-Action Target Rate: 16%, 29%

While Dak Prescott and Pickens didn't start where they left off in'25, at least the strong WR2 role was still there. Along with a bevy of intermediate routes off play-action (which increases receiver efficiency), Pickens was, at worst, a slight overpay. Now, he has Ryan Flournoy (at 5.7 targets per game over his last three) siphoning targets away. Along with being on a team with an outside shot at the playoffs, Pickens' job has somehow diminished and gotten more volatile. Fortunately, after Monday night, there's a clear team in the hunt that could use a WR2.

Cam Lewis delivers a devastating legal hit to Tory Horton!

That's some old school NFL type of power. pic.twitter.com/UIERoXZqVu

— The Goal Line Grind (@theGLgrind) November 3, 2026

Jaxon Smith-Njigba caught six passes for 118 yards and a score. The rest of the Seahawks' WRs totaled 33 yards on four catches. Now, I get it. We're asking too much of Tory Horton and Cooper Kupp. I'm sure Rashid Shaheed's return will set things right. But before we toss the idea of adding Pickens aside, let's take a look at Shaheed's season to date.

  • Target Rate: 14.4%, 53rd (out of 57 qualifiers – min. 25 targets)

  • YPRR: 1.20, 49th 

  • Explosive Play Rate: 35th 

Shaheed had only earned two more targets than Kupp before getting injured. And he had fewer yards. While I enjoy watching the JSN Show each week, a lesser running game only puts more of the onus on Sam Darnold to keep the offense moving. Pulling Pickens into the fold would be the ideal complement in both fantasy and real life. 

Adonai Mitchell to the Chiefs

Thinking back to my Bengals pick for a trade above, Tony Pollard is actually the likelier option. Tyjae Spears' injury has given Tennessee the runway to feature Pollard over the last couple of weeks, and it's worked out well. The former Cowboys even notched his second straight 100-yard game against Cincinnati on its home turf. There's no better way to get a sense of a player's talent than a live audition.

And the Jets have a similar opportunity this weekend. 

Adonai Mitchell set a new career high with 142 receiving yards, topping his previous best of 102.

7 REC, 142 REC YDS, 1 TD vs Raiders

Acquired in the Sauce Gardner trade, Mitchell is showing serious potential in New York. pic.twitter.com/djWO4vT8Ik

— Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) November 1, 2026

Adonai Mitchell came back from injury and stole the show in New Jersey. After a Mason Taylor and Omar Cooper Jr. week, Mitchell relegated those two to role players as he put up the most yards of any Jets pass-catcher in a single game since Week 15 of 2024. But it's not just about his total in the box score. His on-field deployment should interest any team looking for a downfield threat. 

Yes, Mitchell's touchdown catch came on a go route. But Geno Smith connected with Mitchell on multiple timing routes to the outside, along with a deep crossing route for an explosive. He has the size and speed to not only be a downfield threat, but to create separation at the snap. That's something the Chiefs sorely need.

Xavier Worthy was kinda cookin' a couple times in this game. pic.twitter.com/K9UH5flNyF

— Daniel Harms (@InHarmsWay19) November 2, 2026

One-game sample caveat, but against the Broncos, the Chiefs' WRs caught 10 of 11 targets for 62 yards and a score on throws of 10 air yards or shorter. Essentially, the Rashee Rice special. Anything past that resulted in two catches for 24 yards. Actually, Patrick Mahomes doesn't have a TD completion to a WR on an intermediate or deep threat since Week 4. Kansas City balanced the offense with Kenneth Walker III. But with its deficiencies at WR, Sunday's result should be a lesson in becoming a one-dimensional offense that it doesn't want to relearn in January.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings: Week 9 Edition
item.description: ﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿100% accurate ranking of all 32 NFL teams.﻿
item.content:encoded:
Now that Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season is in the books, it’s time for an incredibly meaningful and serious exercise: NFL Power Rankings! What differentiates these rankings from all others is that they’re THE only truly accurate ones in the entire universe. Hard to believe, I know. But it’s true. Let’s take a look at how all 32 teams stack up.

BLG’S WEEK 9 POWER RANKINGS

1 – Chicago Bears (LW: 5) – The Bears going into Seattle and dominating the reigning Super Bowl champions was really impressive. This team looks like a force to be reckoned with, especially after adding Jeffery Simmons to their defense. Overall strong combination of talent and coaching.

2 – San Francisco 49ers (LW: 2) – The 49ers had a solid bye with Seattle (NFC West threat) and Minnesota (No. 1 seed threat) losing. They’ll host a spunky Raiders team in Week 9.

3 – Buffalo Bills (Last Week: 3) – The Bills have lost one game this season and it was by three points to a division rival. As their conference’s only one-loss team, they have a navigable path to the No. 1 seed in the AFC playoff picture.

4 – Kansas City Chiefs (LW: 1) – Make that two straight losses for the Chiefs. This team needs some help ahead of the NFL trade deadline and they’ll probably make some moves to get it.

5 – Detroit Lions (LW: 7) – The Lions are the only NFC North team yet to lose a game in their very competitive division. They continue to be ravaged by injuries but they shouldn’t be slept on.

6 – Minnesota Vikings (LW: 4) – The Vikings weren’t going to stay undefeated with how inept their offense has been. Their defense is going to make teams really earn wins over them, though.

7 – Jacksonville Jaguars (LW: 9) – The Jags own the NFL’s best point differential at +85. The next closest team is the 49ers at +58. Jacksonville also ranks second in DVOA. They’re a real title contender.

8 – Seattle Seahawks (LW: 6) – If the season ended today, which it doesn’t, the Seahawks would actually be on the outside looking in with seven teams ahead of them in the NFC playoff picture. This is still a good team but they’re not an elite team like they were last year.

9 – Cincinnati Bengals (LW: 8) – Despite being 12.5-point home favorites, the Bengals needed overtime to beat the lowly Titans. Not really ideal to allow Cam Ward to log the third-best passer rating of his career against your defense.

10 – New England Patriots (LW: 11) – It has not been a great vibes season for the Pats but they’re 4-1 in their last five games. Drake Maye has thrown 14 touchdowns to two interceptions for a 122.2 passer rating during that stretch.

11 – Los Angeles Rams (LW: 12) – The Rams are benefiting from a softer part of their schedule. It also sounds like Myles Garrett could be back soon. Maybe they’ll make a run.

12 – Denver Broncos (LW: 13) – Unfortunately, Sean Payton is a pretty good coach. The Broncos are tied for the NFL’s best record against the spread this season, a sign that this team is outperforming their expectations.

13 – Las Vegas Raiders (LW: 15) – The Raiders broke their four-game losing streak with a thrilling win over the Jets. Very interested to see how they fare over their next three games: at San Francisco, vs. Seattle, at Denver. That stretch will be a litmus test for just how real this team is.

14 – Green Bay Packers (LW: 16) – The Packers are lacking a signature win over a good team this season. They’ve beaten lesser competition but have yet to come out on top against a big dog. (I’m not counting the Bears game that Tyson Bagent started.)

15 – Pittsburgh Steelers (LW: 20) – Do we have to take the Steelers seriously? They’re currently the top team in the AFC North, though Cincy’s ceiling appears to be higher.

16 – Baltimore Ravens (LW: 10) – Oof. The Ravens are taking a big fall here after losing both Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley to injury. Undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano might start in Week 9 even though he’s banged up as well. Not looking good.

17 – Dallas Cowboys (LW: 14) – The Dallas defense is a joke and Brian Schottenheimer is doing a bad job. That being said, Dak Prescott deserves more blame than he’s getting. The Cowboys actually got a stop in overtime after the Cardinals got the ball first. Only needing to move into Brandon Aubrey’s long field goal range while playing at home, Prescott oversaw a drive that netted -5 yards in three plays and resulted in a punt. That’s a gotta have it moment for the highest paid quarterback in the NFL and he came up extremely small in a huge spot. Hardly the first time!

18 – New York Giants (LW: 18) – The G-Men are returning from their bye as road betting favorites in Philly for the first time since 2009. New York is also looking to boost their roster with more talent ahead of the NFL trade deadline. They just might win the NFC East.

19 – Cleveland Browns (LW: 17) – The Browns had a chance to make people take them more seriously by beating the Steelers in Pittsburgh. They did not come close to making it happen.

20 – Tampa Bay Buccaneers (LW: 22) – Obligatory mention of the Bucs winning in Week 8 despite not completing a pass. The Bucs are perhaps following the 2024 Eagles script of just running the hell out of the ball. Not a bad strategy if teams can’t stop it!

21 – Carolina Panthers (LW: 19) – Two of the three Panthers’ win this season have come against depth quarterbacks (Cooper Rush and Tanner McKee). They’re not scaring anybody.

22 – Atlanta Falcons (LW: 21) – I continue to maintain that the Falcons are the NFL’s most unpredictable team on a weekly basis. They followed up an impressive Week 7 over the 49ers by losing to a team that couldn’t even complete a single pass against them.

23 – Arizona Cardinals (LW: 27) – Minshew Mania is running wild on you, brother! The Cards are one win away from surpassing their 2026 projected win total (3.5 games) with nine games left to play. Props to Mike LaFleur for helping his team overachieve expectations.

24 – New Orleans Saints (LW: 23) – The Saints are returning from their bye to host the Sheuder Sanders-led Browns. We’ll see if Kellen Moore can make a run in a weak NFC South.

25 – Houston Texans (LW: 24) – The Texans are returning from their bye to play the Bolts in California. If Houston can’t win this game, stick a fork in them.

26 – Washington Commanders (LW: 28) – The Commanders didn’t exactly look amazing in a win over the Eagles but, hey, they bought some time to keep their season alive in a weak division. We’ll see if they can build on this victory with the Rams, Giants (massive game in the NFC East), and Bengals up next.

27 – Miami Dolphins (LW 29) – After losing their first three games by double digits, the Dolphins’ last four games have been decided by one possession (1-3 in that stretch). Progress?

28 – New York Jets (LW: 30) – The Jets aren’t good but they’ve at least played some entertaining games this season.

29 – Philadelphia Eagles (LW: 25) – The Eagles are pitiful. I have my doubts that Nick Sirianni is going to survive a failure this massive.

30 – Tennessee Titans (LW: 31) – Taking the Bengals to overtime feels like a moral victory for this group.

31 – Indianapolis Colts (LW: 26) – Tanking doesn’t do the Colts much good since they don’t their own their first-round pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. But they’ll still get higher picks in the other rounds.

32 – Los Angeles Chargers (LW: 32) – Five of the Chargers’ seven losses have come by more than one possession. They haven’t even really been competitive.

Commanders Film Review: Pass Rush vs Eagles

Coming off the bye, they were hoping to turn things around and against the Eagles they certainly did. They delivered five sacks and multiple other pressures. According to NextGenStats, the Commanders had a season-high pressure rate at 46.5%. When they blitzed, they had a pressure rate of 83.3%, the second highest pressure rate on blitzes by any team in the NFL this season.

So how did the Commanders do it? During the bye week, I wrote about some schemes that worked which they could use more frequently, and we definitely saw them come up against the Eagles on Sunday night. Things like read blitzes, disguised overloads and B gap stabs were all effective against the Eagles.

This rush is Chaisson at his absolute best. He’s so quick off the snap and his speed is a real threat to any tackle when he gets it right. Mailata is one of the best left tackles in football and very few rushers beat him for speed, but Chaisson does exactly that here. Chaisson times the snap perfectly and by his second step, he’s already hip level with Mailata. He gets Mailata panicked and forces the tackle to completely turn around to try and stay with him. Mailata gets his outside hand on Chaisson’s shoulder, but Chaisson shows nice bend and dip as he gets under Mailata and turns the corner.

Mailata makes one last effort to save the block by shoving Chaisson, trying to push him beyond the depth of the quarterback, but the quarterback fails to feel the pressure and step up in the pocket. That allows Chaisson to use that shove as momentum to close even quicker. Chaisson lands a big hit on the quarterback, who just about manages to get a throw away before Chaisson brings him down. That throw looked like it might have been intercepted by Nick Cross, but Shy Tuttle got his hand up at the line of scrimmage to knock it down.

Towards the end of the game, Odafe Oweh got in on the action too. Oweh spent most of the game working against Mailata, the Eagles best lineman, so he wasn’t as effective overall as the other rushers. But by getting to work against the same man constantly, he was able to figure out ways to beat him. By the end of the game, Oweh got the better of him.

Overall, the Commanders will of course be happy with the uptick from their pass rush unit in this game. They generated much more consistent pressure and of course finished those plays, putting up five sacks. However, this felt to me much more like the Eagles offensive line being bad than the Commanders pass rush being exceptionally good. Don’t get me wrong, you can only play against whoever the opponent puts out there each week, so I’m not trying to discredit this performance. But I do wonder how sustainable it is.

The Commanders blitzed at a significantly lower rate than they have done all season. Much of these pressures and sacks came on four-man rushes. We’ve seen through the first six games of the season that this pass rush isn’t good enough to consistently win with four, and that Daronte Jones has had to blitz a lot and dial up various pressure packages in order to generate consistent pressure. This game doesn’t line up with that theme so far this season, which speaks to an issue with the Eagles offensive line rather than some big adjustment the Commanders made over the bye week.

Individually, everyone played well up front. Chaisson had perhaps his best game in a Commanders uniform. Omenihu was a menace to whoever had to try and block him on the inside. Armstrong got the better of Bell frequently. Oweh had a solid game against one of the best tackles in the league. While Oweh and Chaisson had some very good reps against Mailata, they’ve had some very good reps individually in lots of games this season and the overall rush unit hasn’t looked this good. So I’m reluctant to say that this group has turned the corner. I definitely believe in their talent and I like the unit overall, but I’m eager to see if they can stack up performances like that against a Rams team with a much stronger offensive line.

So the fact that it didn’t have to be me as the one doing that, I thought was good. Obviously, frustration and all that builds in, so I like it when that happens.”

Johnny Newton’s Commanders return takes on new urgency after Javon Kinlaw surgery

The Commanders thought they had a steal at No. 36 overall in the 2024 NFL Draft, but foot injuries prevented [Newton] from making an instant impression.

They wanted him to become a genuine three-down force. They wanted him to evolve into a franchise cornerstone to build around for the next decade. And they wanted him to silence his pre-draft doubters after his top-15 talent plunged out of the first round entirely.

Commanders shout out Terry McLaurin by copying TD celebration

McLaurin wasn’t on the field or supporting his team from the sideline for their Week 8 Sunday Night Football matchup. Instead, he was watching the Commanders’ divisional game against the Philadelphia Eagles at home, nursing a season-ending torn patellar tendon he suffered while running a route in the first quarter of Washington’s 23-17 loss to the San Francisco 49ers on Oct. 19.

Having been selected as a team captain for the fifth time in his career, McLaurin’s presence as a leader is what his teammates miss most.

Ahead of pregame warmups, Jayden Daniels and Mike Sainristil repped two different styles of tribute shirts that featured photos of McLaurin prominently on both the front and back. The shirts were designed by Dreamathon, an apparel brand that has ties to both McLaurin and the NFLPA.

“Because that’s my dog, and to see him go down kind of hurt all of us,” Williams said in his postgame press conference of the celebrations, “But…we all came together as a receiver group and said we were going to keep spamming the little ‘Scary Terry’ emotes. The Cowboys Are An Embarrassment To Everyone | Mixtape Mini

Blogging the Boys

Nobody knows how to fall apart like the Dallas Cowboys

The Dallas Cowboys are bad at football. That’s a tough reality to live in. For months we have been clinging to the hope that a stellar offense with a gradually improving defense would be the magic ticket to help this team pick up steam and start rolling down the stretch of the season. We have some bad news. Nothing’s rolling.

The defense remains terrible, and the offense has started to join in by underperforming at unpopular moments in the game. The whole thing culminates in disappointing outings and losses to what we think are inferior teams. One after the other.

The latest letdown elevates the frustration to another notch. That’s because it appeared like they were onto something by building a 14-point lead, but things inevitably fell apart. What happened this time? Taking a closer look paints an uncomfortable picture.

With 90 seconds left in the first half, the Cowboys led 14-0. The Cardinals hadn’t scored any points yet. With 90 seconds left in the third quarter, the Cowboys led 17-3. The Cardinals only had a field goal through almost three quarters of football. The defense finished with five sacks and two takeaways. They were making plays, but then they went from playing really well to absolutely horrid. What happened?

This is the frustrating part. The Cowboys got comfortable. Instead of playing disciplined, sound football, they wanted to annihilate the Cardinals and got caught overpursuing. On the big running plays, it was a collection of failures. The defensive line didn’t maintain their gaps. Instead, they were aggressive and attacked upfield. With holes available, the defensive backs took poor angles and completely whiffed with their tackling. Manageable gains turned into monster plays for the Cardinals.

Those two big running plays allowed Arizona to get back in the game because they were fast strikes. And when the Cowboys offense couldn’t finish things on their end, the Cardinals were given more chances to attack, and the defense wasn’t equipped to fend them off.

Blogging the Boys

Brian Schottenheimer is failing the Cowboys

He routinely fails to make the basic decisions that would maximize his team’s probability of winning. One example is his weird habit of running quarterback sneaks down at his own goal line. Instead of trusting his playmakers or scheming an effective play, he plays scared and chooses to waste a down, putting the offense in a tough spot. Every time he does this, the Cowboys have punted three plays later.

Another example is his treatment of Brandon Aubrey. We all know that Aubrey is one of the league’s most lethal kicking weapons, but Schottenheimer finds ways to turn that into a disadvantage for the Cowboys.

Rather than pressing and trying to pick up extra yards to give him a more reasonable field goal attempt, the head coach contentedly runs the ball and settles for a short gain. His confidence in Aubrey treats those situations like an automatic three points instead of working for a shorter attempt. He unnecessarily creates high-stress kicking situations that have resulted in blocks and misses.

The team also cannot stop repeating the same mistakes. They look uncoached at times, committing the same self-inflicted errors week after week. Are we sick of neutral zone infractions yet? Every week. Early and often. It’s just the same penalties over and over. It’s become an epidemic. Whatever the coaches are doing to discourage this practice is not working. They keep jumping early.

For some reason, the team’s most explosive receiving weapons are underutilized. Schottenheimer fails to create mismatches, and the offense becomes very stagnant at times. No pre-snap motion or creative blocking schemes. The Cowboys’ offense has turned into a predictable entity that defenses can absolutely shut down at certain points in the game, and those moments are extremely harmful.

Under Schottenheimer, the Cowboys constantly invent new ways to lose football games. Against the Cardinals, it was the inability to run out the clock. Earlier in the year, against the Ravens, it was a goal-line debauchery that couldn’t win the game. Both instances put the pressure back on a porous defense to come through, and sadly, they did not.

The Cowboys don’t just lose. They actively engineer their own downfall through a blend of situational ineptitude and executive panic.

Philly Voice

How miserable this season already is and will likely continue to be

[At] the end of half sequence, the Eagles had a chance to score some points, but instead punted it away, and the Commanders got points instead. Well, on a 2nd and 6 play during that sequence, Elijah Mitchell caught a pass in the flat and had some room to run along the sideline. When a defender approached he stepped out of bounds. Had he tried to run through contact he would have gotten extra yardage and any contact would have forced him out of bounds to stop the clock anyway. A possible 6-8 yard gain instead became a 4-yard gain, setting up a 3rd down.

On 3rd down, McKee threw an incomplete pass and the Eagles punted. Washington then got a long punt return, followed by a long pass play, followed by a Jayden Daniel scramble, and they kicked a field goal with 12 seconds left in the half.

On the final play of the half, the Eagles ran the injured, pitch-count Barkley into the line before heading to the locker room for halftime.

The postgame explanation was that Sirianni was hoping Barkley could break off a long run and either score or get enough yards to call timeout and kick a field goal.

Barkley has been a soldier this season, but it has to be only a matter of time before he sees this season for what it is and how his body is being compromised for teammates who aren’t matching his toughness, and he concludes, “For who, for what?”

Bleeding Green Nation

10 Eagles things I think I think from the loss to the Commanders

This offensive line has gotten significantly worse under Chris Kuper

Jeff Stoutland might be the best assistant coach in franchise history. The Eagles were never going to replace him.

Unfortunately, the Eagles found an offensive line coach that doesn’t improve his players — at all. Under Kuper, two of the five starting offensive linemen (Landon Dickerson and Tyler Steen) from last season have gotten worse and the two young players (Markel Bell and Drew Kendall) are struggling to improve week in and week out.

Bell was abysmal against the Commanders, allowing a 7.0% pressure rate and two sacks while getting dominated by K’Lavon Chaisson all night.

If the Eagles do decide to move on from a coach this month, Kuper should be the first candidate.

The Eagles were right about Tanner McKee this summer

McKee lost out to Andy Dalton in the battle for the QB2 job for a reason.

There is enough tape in the three games to demonstrate McKee isn’t good enough to be a starting quarterback in the league. Even with the offensive line decimated by injuries and a poor offensive line, McKee is slow in his progressions and has no mobility to get out of trouble.

McKee was abysmal against the Commanders, finishing 23-of-34 for 212 yards with 0 TD, 1 INT and a 72.2 passer rating. He also had a lost fumble in the second half, giving McKee two giveaways on the night. The numbers should have been worse, but 46 passing yards where in garbage time in the final minute to Eli Stowers.

The run defense is making history

Another week the Eagles defense has allowed 100+ rushing yards to an opponent, as the Commanders had 135 rushing yards against a run defense that was supposed to be a strength of this team entering the year.

Instead, the run defense is historically bad — and on the wrong side of history. The Eagles have allowed 100+ rushing yards in each of the first eight games of a season for the first time since 1968, and only the second time in the Super Bowl era.

That 1968 team was one of the worst in franchise history, as the Eagles started 0-11 and finished 2-12. They weren’t even bad enough to get the No. 1 pick that year, and the fanbase booed Santa Claus that December as a result.

This team quit for the second straight week

The Eagles demonstrated a lack of effort again with 1:52 left in the game, when the Commanders went for two in a 25-10 game that was all but decided. The decision was wise by the Commanders, as a conversion gets them up three scores with barely any time left — an outcome that would make it basically impossible for the Eagles to tie the game (yet alone win).

The defensive line didn’t even try to stop Austin Ekeler from going into the end zone. They checked out, much like the team did on several plays throughout last week’s game.

Upcoming opponent – Rams

Turf Show Times

Struggling Rams try another change on special teams

The Los Angeles Rams released Alex Bachman as they continue to try and figure out their special teams. They released Xavier Smith earlier this year. They’re currently using Brandon McManus for field goals and Joshua Karty for kickoffs. The Rams are trying to adjust their special teams.

Are their changes working? Not yet because they keep making changes. So far, McManus has been perfect, but will he deliver in the clutch? How long will Karty be used for kickoffs? Who will be the next return man for L.A.? Will the Rams go with someone who will just catch or someone with upside on the return?

So many questions for the special teams unit, but as of now, Bachman won’t be one of them, and the Rams are still trying to find answers.

Turf Show Times

Rams’ best option to fill gaping WR hole may not be a trade; could it be rookie C.J. Daniels?

The Rams have Puka Nacua, Davante Adams is on IR, and after them there is second-year veteran Konta Mumpfield and veteran Ram Tutu Atwell, but no one has been able to fill the void left behind by Adams, and if Nacua goes down, who can Matthew Stafford reliably throw to?

Rams head coach Sean McVay had heavy praise for receiver CJ Daniels this week, noting that the rookie sixth-round pick has done “a hell of a job” and deserves “more opportunities”. Instead of a big trade, should L.A. just promote from within and give Daniels a starting role alongside Puka Nacua?

McVay has been asked as the trade deadline approaches if the Rams are looking to add to their wide receiver room, and so far, the head coach publicly has leaned more towards a “No” than a “Yes”. Instead, verbally opting to see other players return from injury, and step up on the depth chart.

Enter Daniels, a Day Three pick in the 2026 NFL Draft who the Rams traded up to acquire. Daniels hasn’t accumulated any stats at the NFL level, yet, but McVay hints that Daniels, rather than a trade, could be an answer for the Rams at their receiver position as they move forward.

Where do the Ravens go from here?

Fowler: In the short term, there are several players with lower-cost contracts if the Ravens choose to pursue them. Brissett was with Ravens quarterbacks coach Isaiah Woolfork last season in Arizona. Bears backup Tyson Bagent has familiarity with Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle. And some conversations I had early this week made me think the Colts’ Daniel Jones is at least on the radar. Baltimore could essentially sign him without spending a lot because of his struggles. Jones’ $5.5 million base salary is tradable, and his 2027 guarantees don’t trigger until the offseason. He’s roughly 11 months post-Achilles tear, so perhaps his play improves.

Graziano: My bigger question is a long-term one involving Jackson’s future with the franchise. I believed going into this season that the most important big-picture goal the Ravens had was to get to next offseason with Jackson feeling good about signing an extension that keeps him in Baltimore for years to come. Now that it is apparent that the season isn’t going the way he or they hoped, my focus is trying to figure out what comes next for the Ravens and Jackson.

Fowler: Assuming Jackson is done for the season, his $84 million cap hit in 2027 is an albatross for Baltimore, which could give Baltimore justifiable hesitance about giving him a top-of-the-market extension because of durability concerns. Thursday will mark Jackson’s fourth missed game this season — the fourth time in six seasons he has missed four or more games.

I’m pumping the brakes on the “Lamar played his last down in Baltimore” talk for now. He’s under contract in 2027. But the Ravens must at least now consider life without him.

Sports Illustrated

Albert Breer: The Lions Gave the NFL a Playbook to Combat the Vikings’ Blitz Scheme

The Lions’ offense didn’t exactly crack the code on Brian Flores’s defense Sunday. Detroit scored 19 points and failed to hit 400 yards for a fourth consecutive game.

But what Drew Petzing’s unit did accomplish was playing the game on its terms, based on the chaos Flores’s group endeavors to generate. And that meant prioritizing managing down-and-distance, shifting personnel usage, and driving on the tendencies and rules of the Vikings’ scheme.

First, the Lions put more tight ends and backs on the field than usual—they were in 11-personnel (one back, one tight end) on only 16 of their 68 snaps. Tight end Sam LaPorta played 93% of the snaps. His backup, Brock Wright, played 76% of the snaps, and third-stringer Tyler Conklin played 31% of the snaps. That helped keep the Vikings off-guard presnap, not tipping off who would be in protection.

Second, the backs and tight ends were key in protection, as Detroit would’ve hoped they’d be. Both Jahmyr Gibbs and Sione Vaki were excellent in pass protection, and the Lions deployed Wright and LaPorta in the backfield at times to help with blitzing linebackers.

Third, the Lions leaned heavily on the run game, calling 39 runs to 29 passes. Ultimately, that helped them stay on schedule. On the Lions’ four scoring drives, they never lost yardage on first down, and faced just two third downs with more than seven yards to gain, one of which was a third-and-8 converted with an Amon-Ra St. Brown end-around.

The result was a bushel of statistics that may not matter as much as points, but were pivotal to the Lions dealing the Vikings their first loss. Detroit rushed for 230 yards on 39 carries. The Lions churned out 24 first downs and had 35:43 time of possession.

Essentially, they played offense with a refusal to allow the Vikings’ defense to dictate the terms of the game to them, in a way that gave Minnesota’s group all the respect it deserved.

item.title: The Good and the Bad from the Chiefs’ loss to Broncos
item.description: One positive note and two learning lessons from Kansas City’s loss in Denver.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs lost their second game of the season in Week 8, 28-24, to the Denver Broncos.

Let’s look at one thing that went well and two things that didn’t from the game:

The Good

Emmett Johnson’s performance

Rookie running back Emmett Johnson was the best player on the field for the Chiefs against the Broncos. Johnson finished with five catches for 128 yards, including a 73-yard receiving touchdown. He only got one carry, but it went for 15 yards.

Johnson’s long touchdown was a great design by head coach Andy Reid and staff. The Broncos love to blitz on third downs. They send their nickel on a blitz, hoping to keep Johnson in protection. Instead, the Chiefs have Johnson leak across the formation and run a wheel route. The Broncos screw this coverage up, as one of the defensive linemen, likely the defensive end, should drop and carry Johnson. Regardless, it’s still Johnson on a defensive end in a footrace, and Johnson is going to win that often.

Andy Reid wanted to get Denver’s linebackers in space, and Johnson executed on those plays. The Broncos are in Quarters coverage here against the 2×2 formation for the Chiefs. The boundary cornerback is occupied by tight end Travis Kelce running a 12-yard in route and can’t turn back to the flat quickly enough. Wide receiver Rashee Rice runs an underneath route to occupy the backside linebacker, leaving the other linebacker responsible for covering Johnson in the flat because the coverage was flooded. He had no chance of stopping Johnson, easily getting around him for another explosive play.

I really liked Johnson coming out of Nebraska due to his combination of agility and balance in the hole. This play is a good example of that. Johnson makes the defensive end miss in the hole after right tackle Jaylon Moore whiffs on a block, makes the linebacker miss inside, jukes the safety inside with a deceleration move, spins out of another arm tackle, and gains 15. These types of plays were all over his Nebraska film, and he can do that in the NFL as well.

Johnson is now up to 237 receiving yards on the year. He’s been terrific on third downs this year, which is huge for spelling lead back Kenneth Walker. I would like to see Johnson get into the rotation for carries as well. The case against giving Johnson carries is that it takes Walker off the field, and Walker has a greater chance of getting explosives. However, giving Johnson more carries does save Walker and keep him fresher to get those plays. I would argue that the Chiefs should probably throw the ball less than they do now and feature Johnson and Walker more often in the run game.

The Bad

Andy Reid’s 3rd and 2 play call before the missed kick

There’s been some consternation about Andy Reid’s playcalling in this game, but honestly, I think the Chiefs offense played about as well as you can hope. This team has two shaky tackles against a great Denver pass rush and one NFL wide receiver in Rice against Denver’s top-tier cornerbacks.

Kansas City’s only options were attacking the Broncos’ bad linebackers in coverage, and they did that well. The run game didn’t go as well as you would hope, but they also had a backup left guard — a separate issue for the team. Denver was always going to stop the run better in this game than they did in Week 1, but the Chiefs’ passing game was legitimately good.

That was a huge difference from Week 1, too, when the Chiefs’ passing game was terrible.

That said, I didn’t like this third-and-2 call before Butker misses the kick. Chiefs are in 12 personnel and run a half rollout for Mahomes. Kelce is the #3 receiver and runs the corner clearout route, which doesn’t make sense to me. The play is designed for Jalen Royals and Xavier Worthy to win on whip routes. Royals and Worthy can’t win against man coverage at all and had zero chance of getting open. Wouldn’t it make more sense to have one of those two bad receivers run the pointless clearout route and let Kelce or even Rice have the underneath route? Why are we designing plays for Worthy or Royals?

Mahomes should’ve thrown this ball away, but I don’t like limiting the field on third-and-2; mainly, designing the play for Royals or Worthy is bad. Worthy just does nothing on the field well anymore, and they need to replace him. Hopefully Royals’ snaps go down once Rice gets healthier.

The Bad

Chiefs defending the flats

The Chiefs defense made me mad in this game. Once again, they had zero pass rush. Broncos quarterback Bo Nix did hit some nice downfield throws that weren’t always bad coverage. But the biggest issue was how badly the Chiefs defended the flats.

Bo Nix is either a vertical or flat thrower. He does nothing else. This is the Chiefs’ fifth time facing Nix, and they didn’t seem to realize it.

It started twice on the first drive: the first was a running back screen Alohi Gilman was late to close on, and the second was Cochrane completely lost on a bootleg.

Gilman has to defend Jonah Coleman in the flat here and lets Coleman run past him, and he gets called for pass interference.

The Broncos run a switch release to Waddle for a touchdown. Chris Rolland-Wallace and Nohl Williams botch the switch call, and Rolland-Wallace is way too late to recover on Waddle.

The annoying part is the Chiefs messed this up again, this time off a bootleg. Jadon Canady thinks he’s running the clearout route, but Williams does too, making one of them way too slow in the flat.

The Chiefs send a six-man pressure here with two to the running back side of the protection. The Broncos have six in protection and slide the right way. I believe Nick Bolton is green-dogging here, which means he blitzes if the back stays in protection; otherwise, he has him in coverage. Regardless, he gets lost on the play, and the blitz means everyone is behind the play when it goes for 51 yards.

item.title: Mailbag: Could the Lions target a linebacker at NFL trade deadline?

item.content:encoded:
The NFL trade deadline is now less than a week away. If teams want to add talent via a trade, it must happen by 4 p.m. ET on Tuesday, November 10. After that, the only talent acquisition can come via free agency or waivers.

The Detroit Lions’ interest in a cornerback is no secret. The team openly admitted they were involved in talks for Joey Porter Jr., although the Dallas Cowboys apparently outbid them. Cornerback sure seems like it’s still on the table, but could Detroit’s strategy shift after losing several players to injury on Sunday against the Minnesota Vikings?

With rookie Jimmy Rolder out for the year and All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell out indefinitely with a neck injury, suddenly linebacker seems like a pretty serious need. This week, the Lions have backfilled their depth chart with special teams pieces in KJ Britt and (reportedly) Owen Pappoe. But can they trust players like Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske to hold starting roles? Or do they need to make an aggressive move to raise the ceiling of the room and fortify the middle of the field?

On this week’s Midweek Mailbag podcast, we discuss the Lions’ options at the NFL trade deadline, and outline a couple of names we’d like to see the Lions consider. At the top of that list is undoubtedly Eagles linebacker Zack Baun. The 29-year-old All-Pro linebacker is on a very manageable contract for Detroit (salaries of $1.215M, $1.345M, and $1.39M from 2026-28, plus a $14 million option bonus in 2027). It makes a little less sense for the Eagles (over $16M in dead cap), but if the Lions could make it worth it with draft compensation, they could get a deal done. And with the Eagles 2-6—losers of six straight—forced to play Tanner McKee at quarterback, it may make sense to acquire as much draft captial as possible.

Other linebacker options discussed: Buccaneers’ Alex Anzalone and Dolphins’ Jordyn Brooks.

We also talk about whether the Lions’ strategy should change considering how competitive the NFC North is this year. Does it make sense to get in an arms race with the Chicago Bears after their acquisition of Jeffrey Simmons? Or is that actually a reason to pull back this year and wait for a time in which things feel more open?

And we talk about a lot of topics beyond the trade deadline, including:

  • How the Lions’ “sidecar” formation was the perfect antidote to Brian Flores
  • Why didn’t Ennis Rakestraw play much vs. Minnesota?
  • What’s with the Lions’ short-yardage issues?
  • Is it actually better to have the 5th or 6th seed in the NFC rather than the No. 2 seed?
  • Should the Lions consider extending Christian Mahogany this offseason?
  • How many carries for Sione Vaki is the sweet spot?

Wednesday morning, breaking news emerged on the Cleveland Browns’ quarterback situation as the team placed starter Deshaun Watson in the concussion protocol. The team released the following statement:

During the first quarter of Sunday’s game against the Steelers, Deshaun took a helmet-to-helmet hit. The ATC spotted called down to the sideline, and the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma Consultant (UNC) administered a gameday concussion evaluation. Both times he showed no symptoms, passed his evaluations, and was cleared. If Watson is out, then Sanders would start his first game of the 2026 NFL season. It’s certainly a unique situation for the Browns’ quarterback situation. At the start of the season, many fans wanted Sanders to start over Watson. However, Watson has led five game-winning drives in the team’s 5-3 start to the season, which has led to more fans at least tolerating watching him. The metrics still show he’s been a below average quarterback, though, so if Sanders indeed starts, he’ll have a chance to shift the narrative again to whether he should remain the team’s starter. It probably couldn’t come at a better time, too, because the Saints’ defense is among the worst in the NFL, and the Browns then return home for a four-game stretch.

item.title: Deshaun Watson in concussion protocol. Shedeur Sanders could start as Browns QB
item.description: The Browns placed Deshaun Watson in the NFL's concussion protocol, putting the team's starting QB in jeopardy of missing the team's Week 9 game.
item.content:encoded:
The Cleveland Browns placed Deshaun Watson in the NFL's concussion protocol, putting the team's starting quarterback in jeopardy of missing the team's Week 9 game against the New Orleans Saints.

The Browns announced Watson's placement in concussion protocol in a statement released on Wednesday, Nov. 4.

"During the first quarter of Sunday's game against the Steelers, Deshaun took a helmet-to-helmet hit," the Browns statement read. "The ATC spotter called down to the sideline, and the Unaffiliated Neurotrauma Consultant (UNC) administered a gameday concussion evaluation. Deshaun was cleared by the UNC and returned on the Browns' next offensive series."

"As part of the protocol, the team's medical staff evaluated him again postgame and Monday morning," the statement continued. "Both times he showed no symptoms, passed his evaluations, and was cleared. On Tuesday morning, he reported to the medical staff that he began experiencing concussion symptoms Monday night and was immediately placed in the concussion protocol."

Watson has guided the Browns to a surprising 5-3 record in 2026 while completing 65.5% of his passes for 1,806 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions. If he can't play, backup quarterback Shedeur Sanders will likely be handed the reins against the Saints.

Here's more to know about Watson's injury, the NFL's concussion protocol and how the Browns' quarterback depth chart shakes out behind him.

What is the NFL's concussion protocol?

The NFL's concussion protocol outlines a five-step process for players who have been diagnosed with a concussion to return to action. The steps are as follows:

  • Phase 1: Symptom-limited activity (introduction of light aerobic activity)
  • Phase 2: Aerobic exercise (more than 20 minutes of moderate to strenuous resistance)
  • Phase 3: Football-specific exercise
  • Phase 4: Club-based non-contact training drills (participating in all non-contact practice drills)
  • Phase 5: Full football activity (clearance)

Once a player completes the process and is cleared for full participation by his team's physician, he must also be seen and separately cleared by an NFL- and NFLPA-approved Independent Neurological Consultant (INC). A player cannot return to action until he is cleared by an independent physician.

There is no official timetable for a player to progress through the NFL's concussion protocol, though NBC Sports and CBS Sports report the median recovery for NFL players is about nine days. Such a timeline would put Watson in danger of missing the Browns' Week 9 game, so his practice status will need to be monitored closely.

Will Shedeur Sanders start for Browns in Week 9?

If Watson can't clear the NFL's concussion protocol ahead of the Browns' Week 9 game against the Saints, backup quarterback Sanders would be expected to start.

Sanders, a fifth-round pick from the 2025 NFL Draft, has played sparingly in 2026 after losing the starting job to Watson during the preseason. As a rookie, Sanders completed 56.6% of his passes for 1,400 yards, seven touchdowns and 10 interceptions while leading the Browns to a 3-4 record across seven starts.

Browns QB depth chart

The Browns are one of just a few NFL teams to have four quarterbacks on their 53-man roster. Below is a look at the pecking order within the unit.

  1. Deshaun Watson
  2. Shedeur Sanders
  3. Dillon Gabriel
  4. Taylen Green

Like Sanders, Gabriel was selected in the 2025 NFL Draft. The third-rounder made six starts as a rookie, posting a 1-5 record while completing 59.5% of his passes for 937 yards, seven touchdowns and two interceptions. The lefty missed the start of the 2026 NFL season with a back injury but returned from IR ahead of Cleveland's Week 8 loss to the Pittsburgh Steelers.

Meanwhile, Green – a sixth-round rookie out of Arkansas – has served as the Browns' thrid-string quarterback for most of the season without Gabriel available. The 24-year-old has yet to play an NFL snap.

This story will be updated as more information becomes available.

item.title: 3 Giants-Eagles storylines for Week 9: Can New York handle prosperity?
item.description: The script has flipped in the NFC East.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants head to Lincoln Financial Field, a place that has been a house of horrors for the Giants more than a decade, to face the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.

The script has been flipped in 2026, with the Giants leading the division, while the reeling Eagles enter the game in last place in the NFC East with a six-game losing streak.

Let’s look at some of this week’s storylines.

Who’s the bully now?

The Giants have not beaten the Eages at Lincoln Financial Field since a 15-7 victory on Nov. 27, 2013. The Eagles have won the NFC East title three of the last four seasons, appearing in two Super Bowls and winning one. The Giants went 11-38 from 2023-2025.

Yet, at the midway point of this season we are living in an alternate reality. The Giants are leading the division at 4-2-1 and trying to make moves to improve their chances of reaching the playoffs. They are the betting favorite. The Eagles are trying to figure out what truck ran them over and whether or not Humpty Dumpty can be put back together again.

It is an amazing turn of events.

Question is, can and will the Giants handle their business? Good teams win games like this one.

Who’s toting the rock?

Tyrone Tracy is on injured reserve with a hamstring injury. Cam Skattebo did not practice on Monday due to his own hamstring injury, and head coach John Harbaugh said Skattebo will be “day to day up to the game.” As of this writing, the Giants have not completed a trade for Jonathan Taylor, Derrick Henry, Tony Pollard, Breece Hall, or any other running back. Najee Harris is somewhere looking for a new job.

Devin Singletary, who has 18 carries this season, might be the last man standing from the Giants’ original backfield on Sunday. Gregory Desrosiers will be playing in his first NFL game after being signed off the Los Angeles Chargers practice squad. Practice squad back Phil Mafah has five NFL carries. Eric Gray, released in cuts to the 53-man roster, was just re-signed to the practice squad. He has six fumbles in 81 career touches, hardly a confidence-inspring statistic.

Can J.J. keep rolling?

J.J. McCarthy has played five excellent quarters of football since replacing Jameis Winston in the fourth quarter of a Week 6 loss to the New Orleans Saints. He has fans and media members alike conjuring McCarthy vs. Jaxson Dart scenarios regarding who will quarterback the Giants next season.

There is a long way to go, though, and McCarthy has a lot to prove before putting the Giants into a situation where they would actually have to make such a decision.

Can McCarthy continue to impress? Can he continue to look like a viable NFL starting quarterback? Can he continue to make the Minnesota Vikings silly for dumping him earlier this season in return for the bargain price of a fifth-round pick?

That is to be determined.

McCarthy is actually 7-4 as a starting quarterback with five consecutive victories. The common denominator in all of those games? Just like his national championship-winning career at Michigan, McCarthy was never asked to do too much in any of them.

The Week 7 victory over Houston, when McCarthy went 20 of 28 passing was the most passes he has thrown in any winning effort as an NFL quarterback. The 252 yards passing was also a career-high.

Only twice in his career has McCarthy been asked to throw 30 or more passes. In those two games, both losses, he has gone 36 of 74 (48.6% completions) with 2 touchdown passes and 4 interceptions.

NFL teams will figure out how the Giants are using McCarthy, and how they are orienting their passing attack. Looking at McCarthy’s pass charts at NextGen Stats, it is clear he does not like to throw the ball in the middle of the field. Twenty-seven of his 28 passes against the Houston Texans were outside the hash marks, and most were outside the numbers. The charts from all 11 of his NFL starts tell the same story.

What happens when teams start squeezing the Giants’ passing attack into the middle of the field, where McCarthy doesn’t want to be? What happens when they jam the box and force McCarthy to win games by throwing 35 or more times?

McCarthy’s ability to navigate those things will tell us how much he has truly grown as an NFL quarterback.

item.title: Brandon Aiyuk turns in paperwork to be reinstated, forcing 49ers to make decision on his future
item.description: Brandon Aiyuk hasn't played in an NFL game since 2024.
item.content:encoded:
It's been over two years since San Francisco 49ers wide receiver Brandon Aiyuk played in an NFL game. After sustaining an ACL and MCL injury during the 2024 season, Aiyuk was initially placed on the PUP list ahead of 2025. But his relationship with the 49ers deteriorated, leading Aiyuk to not appear in a game despite still being under contract with the team.

Now the wideout is looking to change that. In an attempt to get back in the NFL, the 28-year-old Aiyuk hired agent Drew Rosenhaus, per multiple media reports. Rosenhaus told reporters he is tasked with "working on getting [Aiyuk] back to work and playing again in the NFL."

Rosenhaus got to work quickly on making that a reality, as it was reported Wednesday that Aiyuk filed paperwork to be reinstated. He plans to report to the 49ers on Friday. At that point, the team has a few options. It can keep him under his current deal, release him or trade him ahead of the deadline, per ESPN.

Aiyuk was previously represented by agent Ryan Williams, but reportedly fired him last November. Aiyuk blamed Williams for the issues between the wideout and the 49ers.

In December, the 49ers placed Aiyuk on the reserve/left team list. He remained on that list as of Wednesday morning, though would presumably be taken off it once his reinstatement papers are processed.

Months after firing Williams, Aiyuk was vocal on social media, often expressing a desire to join the Washington Commanders. Aiyuk and Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels played together at Arizona State for one season. That trade never materialized.

While there were initially questions about how serious Aiyuk was about a return, the wideout answered those Wednesday. His willingness to report to the 49ers on Friday speaks to his desire to finally return to the NFL.

It's also unclear how much interest teams have in Aiyuk. While he proved to be immensely talented in 2022 and 2023, he hasn't played in an NFL game in two seasons and spent the past offseason torpedoing his chances of a return to the 49ers.

Given the injury questions and his personal baggage, Aiyuk might not draw much interest on the trade market.

While the 49ers could use help at wide receiver due to the team's various injuries, it doesn't appear the team is willing to welcome Aiyuk back. When asked about that possibility in September, 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan simply replied "no" when the option was discussed.

Aiyuk is still under contract with the 49ers through the 2028 season. He signed a four-year, $120 million extension with the team in 2024, just months before his season-ending knee injury.
